headline: North Macedonia Parties Share Out Nearly €9 Million from State Budget
author: Sinisa Jakov Marusic
article_body: Supporters of the VMRO DPMNE party wave national flags during a rally at the start of the local election campaign in Skopje, September 2025. Photo: EPA/GEORGI LICOVSKI. North Macedonia’s political parties received almost 9 million euros from the state budget this year for their regular operations, with the ruling VMRO DPMNE party taking a record 2.5 million euros and the main opposition Social Democrats, SDSM, seeing its funding fall by around 40 per cent to about 1 million euros. A BIRN analysis of the 2026 payments , based on data obtained from the Ministry of Justice, shows that the three largest recipients, VMRO DPMNE, the SDSM and the ethnic Albanian Democratic Union for Integration, DUI, together received about 45 per cent of the total funding. Adding in the smaller Levica [Left] and ZNAM parties, more than half of the money went to just five parties. The DUI received about 472,000 euros, down from about 840,000 euros last year. Both falls and rises reflect the parties’ performance in the 2025 local elections and the number of municipal councillors they secured. North Macedonia’s system ties state funding to electoral performance. Thirty per cent of the available money is distributed equally among parties and coalitions that meet a 1-per-cent electoral threshold. The other 70 per cent is allocated according to the number of elected MPs and municipal councillors. This makes local elections particularly important. While parliament has 120 seats, the country’s municipalities have 1,307 elected councillors. In the 2025 local elections, the VMRO DPMNE-led coalition won 548 council seats, compared with 231 for the SDSM-led coalition. “A councillor and an MP are worth the same, so this explains the competition to get as many councillors as possible,” a source from one of the parties told BIRN under condition of anonymity. The system acts as an important financial incentive for smaller parties without any MPs, or even any councillors, as they can still qualify for some state funding simply by passing the 1-per-cent threshold in any single municipality during local elections. In some of the smaller municipalities in local elections, that threshold can be crossed by winning only a few dozen votes. BIRN previously reported on how seven smaller parties exploited this feature to secure more than 80,000 euros each for the following four years. In some cases, such parties run alone in just one, or in a few, municipalities to reach this threshold, while at national level remaining part of coalitions led by big parties. Overall, 62 parties qualified for regular state funding in 2026, the data show, although around one-third of them received less than 20,000 euros. Apart from the almost 9 million euros in annual funding, which consumed 0.15 per cent of the state budget, the state also reimburses party election campaign expenses and provides additional annual funding for the research centres of the four parties with the strongest electoral results. In 2026, an additional 320,000 euros was allocated for those research centres, shared between VMRO DPMNE, the SDSM, the DUI and Levica. The funding comes with obligations, such as submitting annual financial statements and reports and declaring any donations to the State Audit Office, which oversees use of the funds. The law requires the parties to publish these financial reports on their websites by the end of each April. In reality, this requirement is frequently ignored, according to BIRN’s analysis. The State Audit Office told BIRN that the law does not clearly designate who is responsible for monitoring this obligation. Another issue is that parties are not legally required to have an official website. The Audit Office said they have begun discussing digitalisation of parties’ financial reporting, including the possibility of creating a single online platform where all the parties would publish their financial reports.

headline: Montenegro Police Raid Nets 50 Foreigners, ‘Hundreds’ of Digital Devices, and Cash
author: Predrag Milic
article_body: The special state prosecutor’s offices in Podgorica, Montenegro. Photo: EPA/BORIS PEJOVIC Montenegrin police said on Tuesday they were checking on more than 50 foreign nationals, most of them Ukrainian citizens, who they found when raiding a large house in the Mareza area of Podgorica. Police also said they seized hundreds of digital devices, “sophisticated equipment” and a large amount of cash. “Police officers, based on previously undertaken proactive activities, located and identified the facility – a large house in Mareza, Podgorica – after which they entered the building in accordance with the law,” a Police Directorate statement said. According to police, they found more than 50 foreign nationals inside the house and carried out a search of the premises, documenting equipment and other material relevant to the investigation. “During the activities, several hundred digital devices and other elements of sophisticated equipment were found, and their quantity and scale were such that, for adequate relocation, they had to be transported by a cargo motor vehicle,” police said. Police said a large amount of cash was also found and that its origin and possible connection to the activities under investigation would be checked. The authorities said they were examining the legal basis on which the foreigners are staying and working in Montenegro, their activities and movements, the purpose and manner of use of the seized equipment and devices, and any possible links to illegal activities. “Given the complexity of the case, the director of the Police Directorate has formed an Operational Team composed of several groups of police officers specialised in cyber security and high-tech crime, financial investigations and money laundering, international operational cooperation, as well as foreigner and migration affairs, with the strong support of the National Security Agency,” the statement said. Police added that they were taking action in coordination with the State Prosecutor’s Office to establish all the facts and could not comment further at this stage.. “Having in mind the interest of the proceedings and the complexity of the criminal investigation, the Police Directorate is not in a position at this moment to provide more details, so as not to jeopardise the further course of the preliminary investigation,” the statement said.

headline: Suspend Officers Suspected of Beating Serb, Kosovo Police Inspectorate Says
author: Ardita Zeqiri
article_body: Kosovo Police Inspectorate. Photo: BIRN Kosovo’s Police Inspectorate (IPK) said on Tuesday that it had recommended the suspension of two officers following an investigation into allegations made by Nenad Raskovic, a Kosovo Serb, on August 11. Raskovic has alleged that he was physically assault ed by police officers during a raid on his home in the village of Dren, near the northern municipality of Zubin Potok. The inspectorate launched its investigation on August 12 following media reports about the incident. Photographs shared in the media and on social networks show injuries on Raskovic’s back. “Today [Tuesday], the IPK recommended that the Kosovo Police suspend two police officers from the North Mitrovica Regional Police Directorate, suspected of being involved in this case in connection with the criminal offence of ‘mistreatment in the exercise of official duties or public author ity’,” the inspectorate said in a statement. The IPK , an independent institution overseeing police conduct, said further investigative activities will be carried out in cooperation wit h the Basic Prosecution in Mitrovica “to establish the full circumstances of the incident and determine the actions of the police officers involved”. The Belgrade-backed Kosovo Serb party Srpska Lista said on August 11 that Raskovic reported that police officers entered his home in Dren during a raid and, after searching the property, began beating him without explanation. “After that, Nenad was left tied to a tree. With the help of friends, he was freed and taken to the Family Medical Centre in Zubin Potok, and then to the Clinical Hospital Centre in Mitrovica,” said Srpska Lista. Raskovic also made these allegations while speaking to the media from the hospital. He was later sent to Belgrade for further treatment. The Kosovo Police confirmed that Raskovic’s home was among the properties searched during an operation. Erduan Baliqi, a police spokesperson , told BIRN that the searches were conducted as part of an operation related to information about weapons. Srpska Lista called on Western embassies and international organisations, as well as NATO-led KFOR peacekeepers and the EU rule-of-law mission EULEX, to examine the allegations and act within their respective mandates to establish the facts and ensure the rights and safety of the public. Civil society organisations in northern Kosovo, where Serbs form the majority, have also called on the European Union to assess EULEX’s monitoring of the Kosovo Police.

headline: Hungary Narrowly Avoids Full Nuclear Shutdown; Slovenia Plant Still at Full Capacity
author: Marina Zec
article_body: Serbia’s Hydrometeorological Service on Wednesday said the water level in the Danube was either still slightly declining or stable, with a tendency to rise slightly or remain stable over the next four days. However, prolonged low river levels in Serbia generally are creating challenges for the country’s energy sector and fuel imports. Shells are seen on a dry bank of the Danube River in Belgrade, Serbia, 05 August 2026. EPA/ANDREJ CUKIC Ljiljana Krec, director of the Apatin-based public utility company Dunavska Obala, said meteorologists expected a slight rise in the Danube water level, but the situation remained serious. “The situation is far from harmless. It is quite tense, both regarding the pontoons and the boats that have been left stranded on dry ground,” Krec told Serbia’s public broadcaster RTS. A tire is seen stuck on the dried out bank of the Danube River in Belgrade, Serbia, 05 August 2026. EPA/ANDREJ CUKIC The low level of the Danube is especially affecting electricity generation. However, Dusan Zivkovic, director of the Electric Power Industry of Serbia, EPS, told RTS on Wednesday that the electricity supply was stable – and would remain so. “This is a period of major challenges, but I would again emphasise that citizens and businesses should not be concerned about the regular supply of electricity,” Zivkovic said. According to him, electricity generation at the Djerdap hydropower plants has been reduced by the exceptionally low water level, but EPS had prepared the system for such circumstances. He expects the period of low inflows to continue, partly because of limited snowfall in the Alps during the last winter as well as more recent weather. A man cools off in the water at Lido beach on the Danube River in Belgrade, Serbia, 05 August 2026. EPA/ANDREJ CUKIC Due to the low river levels, the supply of petroleum products has become challenging and measures to ensure a stable fuel supply have been stepped up. Serbia’s Minister of Mining and Energy, Dubravka Djedovic Handanovic, met representatives of the Association of Oil Companies of Serbia and the Petroleum Industry of Serbia, NIS, on Wednesday to discuss the transport and delivery of petroleum products amid low water levels on the Danube. Women cool off in the water at Lido beach on the Danube River in Belgrade, Serbia, 05 August 2026. EPA/ANDREJ CUKIC More than half of the 39,000 tonnes of diesel planned for import in August was due to arrive by river. Those deliveries are now uncertain, forcing the authorities to rely on increased domestic production and NIS’s operational reserves. “Imports were reduced to a minimum in July, and we expect a similar situation in August,” Djedovic Handanovic said. She added that the government is “monitoring the water level of the Danube and the availability of rail transport, supervising the situation and taking action to facilitate the delivery of petroleum products wherever possible”. A bird takes off from the shade on the banks of the Danube River in Belgrade, Serbia, 05 August 2026. EPA/ANDREJ CUKIC Following the meeting, the ministry said NIS would release around 23,000 tonnes of its operational reserves to other oil companies and increase daily crude oil processing later in August. A ban on fuel exports would remain in force until the end of the month.

headline: Kosovo Protests as Serbia Mulls Changing River’s Course
author: Perparim Isufi
article_body: Ujman/Gazivoda lake in northern Kosovo accumulates water from the Iber/Ibar river. Photo: BIRN/Denis Sllovinja. Kosovo’s Acting President, Albulena Haxhiu, protested on Monday after the Serbian President announced that Belgrade may change the course of the Iber/Ibar river. Deeming the plan a “serious concern”, Haxhiu said the issue should be addressed with the international community. “As you know, the Iber Lepenc and Ujman [Gazivoda] lake are part of a strategic system for the water supply, energy, agriculture and the lives of hundreds of thousands of citizens of Kosovo,” Haxhiu told the Conference of Ambassadors in Pristina. “A unilateral intervention in transboundary water flows would have consequences far beyond a technical issue, as it would affect the water, energy, environmental and human security of our republic,” she added. Haxhiu spoke out the day after President Aleksandar Vucic of Serbia hinted at the initiative in what he described as justified retaliation against the Kosovo government’s policies towards Serbs in Kosovo. “Since they are harassing our people so much, let’s see, we have various reasons for changing the course of the Ibar, so we’ll see what the Albanians will do and how they will behave,” Vucic said. On Monday, Vucic doubled down on the statement, adding that he was simply “addressing the waterways within the territory of the Republic of Serbia, in accordance with domestic law”. Serbia regards Kosovo as part of its territory and refuses to recognise its independence. Vucic insisted that he was not threatening anyone. “We will simply deal with our own problems. We have our own interests, and we are taking care of our own interests,” he said. This is not the first time Vucic has mentioned the idea of moving the course of the Ibar, which originates in Montenegro, passes through the south-western tip of Serbia and then flows through northern Kosovo and then back into Serbia. After an explosion on the Ibar-Lepenac canal, which supplies several towns through Lake Ujman/Gazivode, in November 2024, Vucic said that the idea of changing the course of the Ibar had existed since 1985. “We can divert the course of the Ibar, and they would be left without Gazivode. Then there would be no lake anymore,” Vucic said at the time. He added that he had always opposed the idea. “I did not want us to use nature for political purposes. After all, we were supplying them with electricity,” he said. On Sunday, Kosovo’s Minister of Environment, Fitore Pacolli, called Vucic’s statements unacceptable. “According to the Helsinki Convention, states have an obligation to cooperate for the fair and rational use of transboundary waters, to prevent transboundary damage and to protect aquatic ecosystems. Water resources cannot be used as an instrument of threat, pressure or destabilisation against another state,” Pacolli said.

headline: Ticket Out: A Serbian’s Journey from Mercenary in Ukraine to Gangland Hitman
author: Maja Bjelos
article_body: Volodymyr Zelensky’s first official visit to Serbia as Ukraine’s president at the weekend was symbolically significant because Belgrade has spent the past four-and-a-half years trying to avoid choosing between Kyiv and Moscow. The visit will inevitably be read as a message to Russia. Some analysts have interpreted Serbia’s intensifying contacts with Ukraine as evidence that President Aleksandar Vucic is edging closer to the West. Yet it is too early to describe this as a geopolitical turn. The visit is better understood as another attempt by Vucic to widen Serbia’s room for manoeuvre while preserving the core elements of his Russia policy: no sanctions and no formal break with Moscow. Zelensky had until now avoided visiting Serbia, wary of the government’s close ties to Moscow, its refusal to sanction Russia and strong pro-Russian sentiment in the country. Nevertheless, a senior Ukrainian official told AFP news agency that Ukraine needed to “pull the Serbs away from Russia”, describing the visit as a blow to Moscow. For the Kremlin, Zelensky being formally received by Vucic weakens the notion that Serbia sits securely within Russia’s political camp. For Brussels, meanwhile, the visit gives Belgrade an opportunity to demonstrate that it can engage constructively with Ukraine even while refusing to align with EU sanctions against Russia. Right-wing politicians in Serbia, however, have warned that the visit could help Vucic strengthen his position ahead of the upcoming elections. Drones on the horizon? Hermes 900, an unmanned aerial vehicle designed for tactical missions that Israel’s Elbit Systems sold to Serbia, displayed at a military parade in Belgrade in October 2025. Photo: BIRN/Sasa Dragojlo. Despite the official announcement that the two presidents will discuss Serbia’s and Ukraine’s European paths, bilateral economic cooperation, and energy, some foreign media outlets suggested cooperation on defence could also be on the agenda. The conservative German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung has reported , without official confirmation, that the visit could involve discussion of a Serbian-Ukrainian drone venture, potentially financed by the United Arab Emirates. Such a project would fit with Serbia’s efforts to expand its drone industry. Earlier this year, Vucic confirmed plans for joint drone production with Israel after a BIRN- Haaretz investigation reported that Israeli defence company Elbit Systems and Serbia’s state-owned Yugoimport-SDPR were planning a factory near Belgrade, with Elbit holding a 51 per cent stake. A Serbian-Ukrainian drone venture will not necessarily follow, but it does show that Belgrade is actively seeking foreign partnerships to develop its capabilities in unmanned systems. For Zelensky, the visit is part of a broader effort to secure support for Ukraine’s war effort across a range of sectors. Energy cooperation and humanitarian assistance are relevant, but so is Serbia’s role in the supply of ammunition to Ukraine through Western intermediaries. US ambassador Christopher Hill told Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung that, early in his posting in Belgrade, the US embassy had determined that Serbian arms producers could supply some of the military supplies urgently needed on the Ukrainian battlefield. Washington subsequently supported purchases of significant quantities of Serbian ammunition. The Financial Times estimated such exports at roughly 800 million euros by mid-2024, a figure Vucic said was broadly accurate. In May 2025, however, he denied that Serbia was supplying Ukraine after Russia’s foreign intelligence service (SVR) accused the Serbian defence industry of “trying to shoot Russia in the back”. Given that the United States played a direct role in bringing Serbia’s defence industry closer to Ukraine – even as Belgrade publicly maintained its policy of military neutrality and refusal to sanction Russia – Zelensky’s visit can also be understood as part of a move by Belgrade to court the Trump administration and demonstrate Serbia’s strategic value to Washington. That effort has become increasingly visible in recent years and has gained further momentum with the launch of the first US-Serbia Strategic Dialogue . Serbian media remains pro-Russian A man holds a split Serbian and Russian flag during a pro-Russia protest in Belgrade, March 2022. Photo: EPA/ANDREJ CUKIC. Serbia and Ukraine have maintained a more functional relationship since Russia’s full-scale invasion than Serbia’s domestic media environment might suggest. From the beginning of the war, Belgrade has formally supported Ukraine’s territorial integrity while refusing to impose sanctions on the Kremlin. Serbia has backed UN resolutions affirming Ukrainian sovereignty, accepted Ukrainian refugees and provided financial, humanitarian and energy assistance. Kyiv, meanwhile, has not recognised Kosovo’s independence, enabling both governments to emphasise reciprocal respect for territorial integrity. Political contacts have steadily intensified. This has included meetings between Vucic and Zelensky on the margins of international summits, visits by senior Ukrainian officials such as Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba’s trip to Belgrade in 2024, and Vucic’s two visits to Ukraine in just over a year. Yet Serbia’s foreign policy abroad and its political communication at home tell different stories. While the government formally describes EU membership as a strategic objective, much of the pro-government media ecosystem continues to cultivate anti-Western, anti-EU and pro-Russian narratives. A 2026 Belgrade Centre for Security Policy study found that the narrative presenting Ukraine as a proxy in a wider Russia-West war was dominant in the Serbian pro-government press between early 2022 and mid-2025. Echoing Kremlin rhetoric, pro-government media portrayed Zelensky as Ukraine’s illegitimate president, while repeatedly depicting the country as subordinate to NATO and the West. Corruption scandals involving Zelensky’s inner circle have likewise been amplified by tabloids to portray the Ukrainian leadership as compromised. The ruling party also echoed “ colour revolution ” rhetoric – that Serbia is being subjected to foreign subversion – through loyal media outlets, to delegitimise and justify the crackdown on mass protests against corruption, growing autocracy and political repression. There have been repeated warnings that the authorities would not allow another “Euromaidan in Belgrade”. Zelensky’s visit creates a domestic communications challenge for Serbia’s president, particularly with his pro-Russian electoral base. The same media ecosystem that has spent years cultivating suspicion of Ukraine and hostility towards the West must now explain why Zelensky is being formally welcomed in Belgrade. For tabloids such as Informer , the crucial message is not what the visit changes, but what it does not. Closer ties with Ukraine, and Zelensky’s visit to Belgrade, do not necessarily signal a shift in Serbia’s policy toward Russia, nor do they imply the introduction of sanctions. Vucic has already stated that Serbia defined its sanctions policy years ago and that this position will remain unchanged. That is also a reason not to read too much into the visit. Just weeks earlier, Vucic was the only leader at a Ukraine-South East Europe summit in Kyiv who refused to sign the joint declaration calling for continued support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia. He also did not attend a ceremony honouring Ukrainians killed in Russia’s aggression. At the same time, Serbia is seeking to deepen economic ties with Kyiv to advance its bid for membership in the World Trade Organization, while continuing arms exports, exploring possible security and defence cooperation, and publicly reaffirming its support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity. This is not necessarily a contradiction, but rather the essence of Vucic’s foreign policy: cultivating relationships with competing powers while avoiding commitments that would foreclose other options. Zelensky’s visit therefore demonstrates to Moscow that Serbia is not exclusively Russia’s partner, while signalling to Brussels and Washington that Belgrade wants to remain geopolitically useful. But unless it is followed by sanctions, substantially greater alignment with EU foreign policy or a structural reduction of Serbia’s dependence on Russia, the visit looks less like a Serbian pivot to the West than another attempt by Vucic to continue his balancing act. Maja Bjelos is a senior researcher at the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy. The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

headline: Land Registry Cyberattack Exposes Holes in Romania’s Digital Defences
author: Marian Chiriac
article_body: Photo illustration: EPA/SASCHA STEINBACH This summer was supposed to mark an important milestone for Stefania Guga. By the end of July, the 32-year-old had hoped to buy a two-room apartment in a newly built complex on the outskirts of Bucharest, fulfilling her ambition of becoming a homeowner, Guga told BIRN. “I wanted to finalise the transaction before August 1 to avoid paying the higher VAT rate. But for more than a week now, everything has been at a standstill, and I still don’t know whether I’ll make the deadline. It’s no longer up to me – the problem lies with Romanian state institutions,” she said. Guga’s plans have been disrupted by a cyberattack on July 14 targeting the IT infrastructure of Romania’s National Agency for Cadastre and Land Registration, ANCPI, effectively freezing property registration services and real estate transactions. For Guga, the timing could hardly be worse. Under the government’s latest fiscal package, the VAT rate for newly built homes will rise from 9 to 21 per cent on August 1. If she misses the deadline, it will significantly raise the overall cost of her apartment, adding thousands of euros to the price. The ANCPI has described the cyberattack as “the most serious technical incident in the institution’s history”. It crippled the agency’s digital systems, disrupting online land registry services, official email communications and apps used daily by notaries, lawyers, cadastral surveyors and ANCPI staff. Authorities were left unable to register new property transactions, process pending requests, or issue essential land registry documents, bringing much of Romania’s real estate market to a standstill. Just one day after the agency’s systems were compromised, some of the stolen data appeared for sale on a well-known hacking forum. The leaked files included employee login credentials, internal documents and technical information about the agency’s IT infrastructure, raising concerns that the attackers had gained deep access to critical systems. Experts say that, although the attack did not look particularly sophisticated from a technical standpoint, its consequences are serious. “This is arguably the most severe cybersecurity incident in Romania’s relatively short history of the digitalisation of public administration,” said cybersecurity expert Andrei Avadanei. “It affects data belonging to infrastructure classified as critical national infrastructure, including records covering every property in the country. “It has disrupted essential public services and directly affects hundreds of thousands of citizens whose property transactions and administrative procedures are now vulnerable,” he added. Avadanei also said the incident could likely have been prevented if the ANCPI had invested more consistently in cybersecurity and implemented stronger preventive measures. The agency’s spending priorities appear to reinforce that criticism. According to media reports , ANCPI has invested around 710 million lei, or about 135 million euros, in digitalisation over the past two decades. But only about 0.2 per cent of that, roughly 305,000 euros, was allocated to cybersecurity. Experts say that figure is woefully inadequate given the sensitivity of the data the agency manages and its role in operating one of the country’s most critical public databases. Officials have sought to reassure the public and limit the fallout from the cyberattack. In a statement, ANCPI said the incident “did not compromise the agency’s technical or legal databases” and stressed that core land registry records were neither altered nor destroyed. The agency also said it has begun migrating its applications to the Romanian Government Cloud, a process expected to be completed on Wednesday. Once the migration is finished, specialists will carry out comprehensive integrity checks before services are gradually restored. At the same time, the incident has exposed the fragility of Romania’s public digital infrastructure at a time when the country is facing a sustained wave of cyber threats linked to the broader security environment created by Russia’s invasion of neighbouring Ukraine. Romanian authorities and cybersecurity experts have repeatedly warned that government institutions, critical infrastructure and public databases have become attractive targets for hostile cyber actors. “This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire public administration,” interim Digitalisation Minister Irineu Darau said in a televised interview . Darau acknowledged that the digitalisation of Romania’s public institutions has been carried out in a fragmented way, without a coherent national strategy or common security standards. “It is time to make digital transformation and cybersecurity genuine national priorities,” he said. “That also means offering better salaries to cybersecurity professionals working in the public sector so that state institutions can attract and retain the expertise needed to protect critical systems,” he concluded.

Kosovo’s Police Inspectorate said on Wednesday that it was investigating reports published on August 11 claiming officers used excessive force against a Serb man, Nenad Raskovic, during a raid at his home near the northern municipality of Zubin Potok. Photographs shared on media and social networks show injuries on Raskovic’s back. The Police Inspectorate, IPK, said it had interviewed Raskovic at North Mitrovica Hospital, where he is receiving treatment. “The IPK has initiated this preliminary investigation with the aim of verifying the allegations and clarifying all relevant facts and circumstances related to the case,” the Inspectorate, an independent institution overseeing police conduct, said in a statement. The Inspectorate said it would take all necessary steps, including “cooperating with relevant institutions, obtaining official documents and information, and interviewing people who may have knowledge of the incident”. The Belgrade-backed Kosovo Serb party, Srpska Lista, said Raskovic said police officers entered his home in Dren village on Tuesday and, after searching the property, began hitting him without explanation. “After that, Nenad was left tied to a tree. With the help of friends, he was freed and taken to the Family Medicine Centre in Zubin Potok, and then to the Clinical Hospital Centre in Mitrovica,” the party said. In interviews given to media from hospital, Raskovic alleged that he was beaten by Kosovo police. The Srpska List party called on Western embassies and organisations, NATO-led peacekeepers in KFOR and the EU rule-of-law mission EULEX to “examine the allegations and take action within their respective mandates to establish the facts and ensure the rights and safety of citizens”. Petar Petkovic, head of the Serbian government’s office for Kosovo, also posted photos of the alleged injuries inflicted by Kosovo police on Tuesday, saying that “these are photos of [Kosovo Prime Minister Albin] Kurti’s ‘democracy’. “For weeks, months and years, we have been warning the entire international community about the persecution of Serbs by Kurti’s regime, which has led to this. When those responsible face no sanctions and there is no adequate protection, these are the consequences,” Petkovic wrote. Kosovo Police confirmed searching Raskovic’s home. Erduan Baliqi, a police spokesperson for the North Region, told BIRN: “Raskovic’s house was among the properties searched during the operation in Dren village… The searches were related to information on weapons.” Baliqi said the police had “no information about the use of violence”. Civil society organisations in Serb-majority northern Kosovo have called on the European Union to assess EULEX’s monitoring of the Kosovo Police. “These allegations require an urgent and independent investigation, as well as an appropriate response from the relevant institutions,” they said in a statement. The allegations come as attention focuses on war-related crimes in the Zubin Potok area, where excavations have been carried out in several villages in search of mass graves. So far, remains believed to belong to four people have been exhumed, while three people have been arrested on suspicion of war crimes against civilians.

headline: Romania Cuts Industrial Output to Ease Power Shortage
author: Marian Chiriac
article_body: Bucharest residents cool off on one of the hottest days of August by passing through a water-spraying device installed in the city centre, August 3, 2026. Photo: EPA/ROBERT GHEMENT More than 80 of Romania’s largest energy-intensive companies, including car manufacturers, steel producers, fertilizer plants and other major industrial consumers, are to begin maintenance work or scale back production from Tuesday, to ease pressure on the national power grid. The measures come as a prolonged heatwave drives electricity demand to seasonal highs while severe drought has sharply reduced hydropower generation and affected operations at Romania’s only nuclear power plant, at Cernavoda, on the Danube River. Car plants operated by Renault-owned Dacia and Ford are to temporarily halt production until August 19, voluntarily cutting electricity consumption by around 200 MW. Major wood-based panel manufacturer Kronospan will gradually suspend part of its production, reducing electricity consumption by up to 50 per cent, BIRN has learned. The measures follow a government meeting with representatives of the largest industrial consumers on Monday at which interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan urged companies to reduce or reschedule electricity consumption, particularly during the evening peak hours. “We are facing a regional energy crisis. Between 7 p.m. and 11 p.m. we have a significant electricity deficit, which we are covering through imports,” Bolojan said. He also called on households, local authorities and public institutions to voluntarily reduce electricity consumption during the evening peak. He added that Romania had discussed emergency electricity imports with Ukraine, including possible supplies from one of the country’s nuclear power plants. The government declared a nationwide alert in the energy sector on July 31 for the entire month of August, citing severe drought and exceptionally low water levels in the Danube and other rivers. Romania’s sole nuclear power plant at Cernavodă shut down one of its two reactors late last week. The continuing fall in the Danube’s water level is also threatening the plant’s second reactor, raising the prospect of a further drop in domestic electricity production. The Cernavoda plant supplies around one-fifth of Romania’s electricity. In an emergency operation on Monday, the Romanian Navy detonated a massive rock formation obstructing the flow of water towards a Danube branch supplying the Cernavoda plant. Authorities hope the intervention will allow the remaining reactor to continue operating beyond the four to five days it was expected to remain online if water levels continued falling at the current rate. Low water levels on the Danube are expected to continue threatening operations at Cernavoda at least until mid-August. Energy experts say the authorities’ decision to reduce electricity consumption by both industry and households should help stabilise the system in the short term. However, Romania lacks a coherent national energy strategy, according to energy expert Ciprian Cherciu. “Romania should have invested more in refurbishing its hydropower plants and building new generating capacity, as well as in expanding wind and solar energy, which could provide an alternative when the nuclear plant cannot operate at full capacity, as is the case now”, Cherciu said. “Above all, Romania should have invested in developing electricity storage capacity. This is an area where the country remains significantly underdeveloped”, he added.

headline: No Subsidies for Hormone Therapy for Trans People in Albania
author: Ilda Hoxha
article_body: A rally in Tirana for the International Day against Homophobia and Transphobia, May 2017. Photo: EPA/MALTON DIBRA. Albania’s new guideline for gender-affirming hormone treatment for transgender people within the public healthcare system does not provide financing from public funds, according to information gathered by the NGO LGBT Alliance. This means that people receiving such treatment cannot obtain their medications free of charge, Xheni Karaj, head of the LGBT Alliance, told BIRN. “The guideline regulates the provision of healthcare and the clinical protocol, but it does not provide for the reimbursement or public provision of hormones,” Karaj said. The adoption earlier this year of the Clinical Practice Guideline on hormone treatment for trans people sparked a wave of hate speech targeting the LGBTQ+ community, with various posts claiming that the medication would be funded by taxpayers, and that treatment would be made available to minors. However, official documents and responses from the Ministry of Health make it clear that the guideline does not provide for hormone therapy for minors or fund treatment for people over the age of 18. The guideline sets out the clinical procedures to be followed by the Endocrinology Service at the Mother Teresa University Hospital Centre in Tirana for the enrollment and monitoring of people seeking treatment. Evidence gathered by the LGBT Alliance shows that, even for adults covered by the pro tocol, the actual provision of the services exists only on paper. “Although the Clinical Practice Guideline has been approved and entered into force, in practice there have been obstacles that have made it impossible for transgender people to actually access this service,” said Karaj. “The first three cases that were referred received contradictory information from the responsible institutions, which indicates that the guideline is still not being implemented uniformly,” she added. The Mother Teresa University Hospital Centre, the Deputy Health Minister Eugena Tomini and the head of the Endocrinology Service Agron Ylli did not respond to requests for comment on the issue. According to the Ministry of Health, the guideline was developed as part of the measures envisaged in the National Action Plan for LGBTQ+ people from 2021 to 2027 and aims to improve access to inclusive, safe healthcare services based on international standards. “The guideline was developed in cooperation with experts in the field, representatives of healthcare institutions and civil society organisations, with technical support from the Council of Europe,” the ministry said. Karaj said that the transgender community had not been directly informed about the approval of the guideline, and that another issue that remains unclear is the referral pathway to the Endocrinology Service. During the drafting of the guideline, Karaj said, the possibility of direct referral to the Mother Teresa University Hospital Centre had been discussed in order to avoid the barriers or discrimination that members of the community have reported at health centres. However, in the first cases reported to the LGBT Alliance, they were instructed to go through their family doctor first.

headline: Greeks Fear for Fate of Historic Athens Cinemas
author: Eleni Stamatoukou
article_body: No one could have imagined that the Odyssey , the great epic poem by the ancient Greek writer Homer, would one day become the cause of a major battle in the American “culture wars” more than two-and-a-half millennia later. The reason is the casting of a new film by the multi-award-winning British-American filmmaker Christopher Nolan – of Oppenheimer, Dunkirk and Inception fame. Nolan has made a Hollywood fantasy-epic version of the story of the ten-year adventure-filled journey of the legendary Greek king Odysseus back to his homeland, Ithaca. The cast of The Odyssey includes the Oscar-winning black Kenyan-Mexican actress, Lupita Nyong’o, who will play the dual roles of Helen of Troy and her sister, Clytemnestra. The well-known mixed-race American actress Zendaya will play the ancient Greek goddess of wisdom, Athena, while Matt Damon stars as Odysseus. The casting also includes trans Canadian actor Elliot Page and American rapper Travis Scott. But it’s the selection of Nyong’o for the role of legendary beauty Helen of Troy that has provoked the strongest reactions. Matt Walsh, an American conservative political commentator and podcast host, claimed on X that no one thinks Nyong’o is the most beautiful woman in the world, and called Nolan a coward because he “knows that he would be called racist if he gave ‘the most beautiful woman’ role to a white woman”. The Tesla boss and the world’s first trillionaire, Elon Musk, known for his far-right, anti-woke agenda, commented approvingly on Walsh’s post, stating : “True”. In other posts, Musk wrote accusing Nolan of “pissing on Homer’s grave. Disgraceful”, adding that he had “grossly insulted the Greek people. Shame on him.” Christopher Nolan poses with his Oscars at the Academy Awards ceremony in Los Angeles, March 2024. Photo: EPA/ALLISON DINNER In a post commenting on the rules that the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has put in place for the Oscars since 2024 to encourage diversity, Musk also accused Nolan of “wanting the awards, which is why he chose Nyong’o”. Back in Greece, however, reactions have been more nuanced, The far-right Niki [Victory] party asked the Minister of Culture, Lina Mendoni, in parliament both about the choice of Nyong’o but also about the state subsidy of 6.5 million euros for the production of the film, scenes for which were shot in Greece, specifically in the Peloponnese. In an interview , Mendoni stated that the film was financed through a meritocratic process, “just as happens with all international productions”, adding that it is not the state’s job “to dictate to a creator how to artistically render a work or a myth”. Some Greek experts, meanwhile, told BIRN that US right-wingers are trying to take ownership of the way Greek antiquity is interpreted and use it for their own purposes. Dimitris Plantzos, professor of Classical Archaeology at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, EKPA, said that what is essentially being contested here is “who considers themselves to own antiquity, who has the right to interpret it and with what image we imagine it today”. “There is vulgar political criticism [of the Nolan film] coming from people who have absolutely nothing to do with art, who are mobilised solely because they believe … that what they hold sacred and inviolable has been offended – such as the skin colour of the characters in Greek mythology,” added Aristides Hatzis, professor of Legal Theory at EKPA. “These views are ridiculous and dangerous,” he asserted. Figure of poetic construction Matt Damon as Odysseus in ‘The Odyssey’, written, produced, and directed by Christopher Nolan. Photo: OdysseyMovie/Facebook The Odyssey , which consists of 12,110 verses, is not only a story about Odysseus’ return to Ithaca but also a story about the feeling of “nostos” [the Greek word for homecoming] and of humans struggling to find themselves. The central hero is Odysseus, not Helen of Troy, who appears in only two rhapsodies. Helen is not a historical person but “a figure of myth, a poetic construction”, explained Plantzos, adding: “That is why every era remakes her”. “The myth lives precisely because it is translated, distorted and interpreted in the end, and the reason we are talking about it today is this, and not simply because Nolan decided to make a movie,” he said. Plantzos pointed out that the row over the film’s casting reflects today’s concerns rather than those of ancient Greece. “The angry demand that Helen be white says more about us, about our current cultural anxieties, than about Homer,” he noted, adding that “Greek antiquity was never pure and nationally homogeneous”. The myth of Helen was transferred to Greek tragedy by the ancient poet Euripides, who presented her as an idol, and later addressed by Hellenistic literature, painting, opera – and now, by Hollywood. In ancient Greek drama, Helen would have been played by a man, as all women’s roles were at the time. Yorgos Zois, an award-winning Greek director based in Athens, said that Nolan’s casting represents a typical director’s desire to add their own touches to the adaptation of the story – “doing something that has never been done before”. Zois is not an admirer of Nolan, and is not interested in Nyong’o’s skin colour but how or whether “she will embody the role with very strong acting that will touch my heart. “The rest I don’t care about,” he said, explaining that the skin colour argument mainly concerns extremists “who believe in the purity of the roles of the white race”. SpaceX and xAI CEO Elon Musk at the World Economic Forum in Davos, January 2026. Photo: EPA/GIAN EHRENZELLER The motives of the ‘culture war’ instigators is also questioned by Greek film critic Konstantinos Kaimakis, who believe it is “ridiculous to think that Elon Musk and his kind have sensitivity for Greece and Greek heritage”. Hollywood has its own rules, the rules of the market, but it remains a space that is much more progressive “than what Musk and his kind can tolerate”, Kaimakis argued. Kaimakis also said he sees Nolan as a special artist, and believes we will not see “a typical reading of the Odyssey ” in the film. If it’s a masterpiece, the conversation about Helen will stop right there, he predicted. If it is mediocre, however, “the reactions and the language that will potentially be used by his opponents will intensify and be even stronger and harsher”. The angry reactions to Nolan’s choice for Helen are less about Greece than about American concerns about race, said Angelos Chrysogelos, associate professor of international relations at London Metropolitan University. This inevitably misses the essence of “what ancient Greece means to us ourselves culturally and historically”, Chrysogelos added. He also noted the lack of Greek actors in the film’s major roles. Plantzos pointed out that “a black Helen does not alter Homer” – but it does reveal how much we have become accustomed to imagining antiquity “through newer European, often racialised, not to say racist, filters”. The question for Plantzos, who is eager to see the film, is whether the choice of casting achieves something “substantial” or remains “a superficial gesture of diversity”. The issue is whether Nolan will be able to “transform Homer into vital, modern, contemporary, restless cinema”, he said. “We need that. We want that. We are longing for that.”

headline: Letter from Washington: US Seeks to Score Material Goals in the Balkans
author: Enes Hodzic
article_body: Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Republika Srpska entity has spent almost as much on lobbying in the United States since Donald Trump’s return to the White House in January 2025 as during the previous three years combined, BIRN and the business-focussed Bosnian investigative media outlet Capital can reveal. Trump’s second term as US president has been a boon for Bosnian Serb strongman Milorad Dodik. In October last year, Washington lifted sanctions imposed on Dodik three days before Trump’s first inauguration in January 2017 and later expanded to 47 individuals and companies connected to him. The US had deemed Dodik, who has frequently threatened secession for the predominantly Serb-populated Republika Srpska, a threat to the territorial integrity of Bosnia and to the three decades old peace deal that the US brokered to end the 1992-95 Bosnian war. In an abrupt turnaround, Dodik, a former Republika Srpska president and leader of the ruling SNSD party, is now viewed by the Trump administration as sharing its conservative values, and a man willing to open up Republika Srpska to US investment. The change in treatment has coincided with a significant uptick in lobbying by Banja Luka: since the start of Trump’s second term in January 2025, the entity has spent some 2.38 million euros on lobbying in the US, adding four new lobbying firms to its previous two and engaging individuals with close ties to the US president. That compares with 2.39 million euros spent in 2022-2024, after Washington tightened sanctions on Dodik and expanded the list of blacklisted individuals and firms, according to an analysis of documents under the US Department of Justice’s Foreign Agents Registration Act, FARA. Tanja Topic, a political analyst in Banja Luka, said the spending had benefitted the sanctioned individuals, not the entity or its people. “It brought significant benefits to all officials, companies and family members [of Dodik] who has been ‘blacklisted’ in the US for years,” Topic told BIRN/Capital. “Politically and financially, they got a new lease of life precisely thanks to the lobbying activities.” Lobbying effort follows sanctions Member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina Zeljka Cvijanovic (L) and former President of Republika Srpska Milorad Dodik (R) attend a military parade in Belgrade, Serbia, 20 September 2025. Photo: EPA/ANDREJ CUKIC. In 2021, under the Democrat administration of President Joe Biden, lobbyists hired by the Republika Srpska authorities were focussed mainly on forwarding messages from Banja Luka to US senators, including Marco Rubio, now US Secretary of State. In early 2022, however, the focus shifted to direct conversations with, for example, Robin Brooks, the then director of the Department of Human Rights and Humanitarian Affairs at the US State Department and Republican congressman Robert Aderholt. “Our goal is a network of relevant interlocutors who share key principles: respect for Dayton, appreciation of reality, and readiness for rational cooperation,” said Ana Trisic Babic, director of the Office for International Cooperation of the Republika Srpska. Trump’s return to office in January 2025 brought a significant hike in spending by the Republika Srpska in the US. Since then, the entity has hired four new lobbying firms: Zell & Associates International Advocates, Stokes Strategies, GS2Law and Continental Strategy. Zell & Associates International Advocates was paid around a million euros, though almost half of that went to an Israeli subcontractor called Gilad Government Relations and Lobbying. One of the most influential lobbying firms in Israel, Gilad is co-owned by Ariel Sender, who headed Trump’s campaign among US citizens in Israel during the 2016 and 2020 elections; in 2012, the Israeli parliament, or Knesset, temporarily revoked the entry passes for Gilad staff amid an ethics scandal. Zell & Associates did not respond to a request for comment. Republika Srpska also paid around half a million euros to Stokes Strategies, whose submissions to FARA show it focussed on building relations with conservative organisations and meetings in Congress. Stokes paid Christine Czerjenewski of Firefly Communications some 50,000 euros for research work. Czerjenewski has connections in US conservative circles and the Republican Party and is a former fellow of the conservative public policy group The Heritage Foundation, described by The New York Times this week as a “bastion of American conservatism”. Neither Stokes Strategies nor Firefly Communications responded to requests for comment. A month before the US lifted sanctions on Dodik & Co, Republika Srpska authorities hired GS2Law to the tune of 130,000 euros. According to their FARA report, GS2Law was tasked with legal research and preparation of a lawsuit “in connection with the previous listing of certain citizens and entities of Republika Srpska on the OFAC [sanctions] list”. GS2Law did not respond to a request for comment. Continental Strategy was hired earlier this year, on a contract worth around 660,000 euros. The firm is led by former Trump adviser Carlos Trujillo. ‘Convincing arguments’ Under Trump, the US revoked sanctions against Dodik and linked companies and individuals. Photo: EPA/AARON SCHWARTZ. Trsic Babic framed the sanctions as punitive measures against Republika Srpska as an entity. Lobbying alone did not get them lifted, she said, while arguing that some small European states such as Estonia, Latvia or Slovenia spend far more. “It brings access, but the outcome depends on the strength of the case you make,” she told BIRN. “There is no successful lobbying without convincing arguments.” “If we add to that the fact that the results are visible, from the de-escalation of the narrative to the formal lifting of sanctions, then it is clear that quality argumentation has increased the effect of every dollar invested. In other words: the goal was not to ‘spend’, but to prove. And we proved it.” Washington consultant Todd Prince, an expert on FARA reports, said the US firms hired by Banja Luka faced a difficult task. Dodik and his allies were considered “politically toxic” in the US, he said. “Lifting U.S. sanctions on an entity or person has historically been very difficult so the fact that the Trump administration agreed to do so would seem to indicate that the lobbying effort was successful,” Prince told BIRN/Capital. “Considering all the other issues on the Trump administration’s plate since 2025 – tariffs, DOGE, China trade talks, Iran, Ukraine war, etc – it is notable that they found time to address the sanctions removal issue.” Bosnian lobbying Bosnia as a state has spent far less on lobbying. According to reports filed with FARA, the Bosnian American Alliance, BAA, was registered on April 28, 2025, as an agent of the Bosnian foreign ministry. According to its website, the BAA is a US-based NGO dedicated to building relations between the US and Bosnia. In March last year, it signed a contract with the Bosnian foreign ministry, which stated that the BAA would provide its services for free. Media reports have previously highlighted issues in BAA funding, after contributions from a number of private firms were returned due to suspicions of money laundering. Prosecutors in Bosnia reportedly launched a probe and Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic said he had been questioned as a witness in the case. It is not clear what the outcome was. Neither the public prosecution nor the foreign ministry responded to requests for comment. In submissions to FARA, BAA said it had never received any payments or financial compensation from the Bosnian foreign ministry and that its activities were carried out on a voluntary basis. These activities included meetings with US government officials, including at the State Department, the National Security Council, and members of Congress to discuss cooperation and potential trade missions in the fields of critical minerals and liquefied natural gas. BAA, which did not respond to requests for comment, also hired Continental Strategy for a fee of 122,000 euros for US government relations services. Continental Strategy also did not respond to BIRN/Capital questions.

headline: Romania Shuts Nuclear Reactor on Danube as Power Crisis Deepens
author: Marian Chiriac
article_body: River vessels transporting goods pass the Cernavoda Bridge while traveling along the Danube Black Sea Canal in Romania, 5 August 2026. Photo: EPA/ROBERT GHEMENT. Romania shut down its last operating nuclear unit on Thursday as record-low Danube water levels threatened the cooling system at the Cernavoda nuclear power plant, adding to concerns over electricity supplies during a prolonged heatwave. The shutdown leaves both reactors at the country’s sole nuclear plan offline. Cernavoda normally accounts for about 20 per cent of Romania’s electricity production. Officials say the closure will not significantly affect Romania’s energy situation. “Shutting down the last reactor is a controlled process that will only last about 10 days … during this time, Romania will have the resources to cover the energy deficit in the grid,” Romeo Urjan, director of the Cernavoda plant, said. The Energy Ministry in a statement said higher wind power production is expected, while a coal-fired power unit is also due to restart. Authorities are also preparing to increase electricity imports, mainly from neighbouring Bulgaria and Ukraine, to maintain supplies and avoid disruption, as demand remains high in the extreme temperatures. The government has already urged households and businesses to reduce electricity consumption during peak evening hours until the end of the month, to ease the pressure on the power system during the ongoing heatwave. More than 80 large industrial consumers have either reduced production or scheduled maintenance to cut electricity use, while restrictions have also been imposed on water use for agricultural irrigation. The exceptionally low Danube levels have affected river transport, tourism and the energy sector. The government declared a nationwide energy alert on July 31, which will remain in force throughout August. The energy crisis has also fuelled a surge in conspiracy theories and fears that Romania could face a nationwide blackout. Energy experts, however, doubt such a scenario. “People have no reason to fear; they will not be left without electricity. Romania will resort to imports when necessary … though these will be more expensive because all countries in the region need electricity during the same evening peak hours,” energy analyst Corina Murafa said. Murafa warned that higher electricity costs for consumers could be a likely consequence of the situation, as Romania relies more heavily on imports while domestic nuclear generation remains suspended. While the shutdown at Cernavoda is not expected to last long, continued heat and low Danube levels could keep pressure on the country’s energy system for some weeks.

headline: Albania Ruling Party Documents Highlight Country’s Ageing Demographic
author: Blerina Gjoka
article_body: Pensioners in the park in Skenderbej Square in the centre of Tirana. Photo: LSA. Documents produced by governing Socialist Party experts for a reform of the country’s municipal set-up, seen by BIRN, reveal an ageing population that could have adverse economic consequences for Albania. The “Administrative-Territorial Reform 2.0” documents, prepared by experts on a special parliamentary committee, also show how emigration and internal migration have emptied out small towns and rural areas while concentrating the population in a few urban centres. At one end are several urban centres where both population and economic activity are increasingly concentrated. At the other end are peripheral areas, particularly in the northeast, southeast and mountainous regions, which are caught in a vicious cycle of population decline and subsistence economies, with few formal jobs. In these areas, municipal budgets survive largely on central government transfers, with funds often used mainly to cover the salaries of local administration staff. The Urban Mass Index, UMI, one of three analytical documents underpinning the proposed new map of 46 municipalities – which would merge 15 local government units with larger municipalities – documents the territorial transformation of Albania since the 1990s, with a few centres continuing to grow as an increasing number of municipalities lose residents. The “dependency ratio” in the index, which measures the burden that children and elderly people place on the working-age population, shows that in 51 municipalities out of 61 in total, this burden is higher than the national average. In many of them, the number of elderly residents exceeds the number of children. The data highlights an Albania divided into three distinct realities: a small group of municipalities that continue to attract population and economic activity; a group of municipalities with intermediate potential; and a majority of the country’s territory, which is losing the critical mass of population needed to sustain local economies and public services. The analysis is based on data from the 2023 census and, as part of the technical report accompanying the reform proposal, suggests that Albania is experiencing a growing concentration of its population in an ever-smaller number of urban centres, while the rest of the country is losing residents, functions and development capacity. The index results show that only 13 municipalities are classified as having a high level of urban mass and are home to 62.5 per cent of the population. By contrast, 30 municipalities – covering almost half of the country’s administrative map – are classified as having a low level of urban mass and account for just 14.2 per cent of the population. Another 18 municipalities fall into the intermediate or medium category. According to the data, the country’s population is concentrated in the capital, which is home to more than half a million people, followed at a considerable distance by the municipalities of Durres, Vlora, Elbasan, Shkoder, Fieri, Kamza and Berat. At the other end of the scale, municipalities such as Pustec, Libohova, Himara, Kelcyra, Memaliaj, Selenica, Dropull, Finiq, Delvina and Kolonja have the smallest populations. The ruling-party experts did not build the index solely on population size. It also combines other indicators, including population density, the spatial distribution of residents, the demographic dependency ratio and the level of urbanisation. This means that a municipality may cover a large area, but if its population is concentrated in a small town while the rest of its territory is largely empty, it is considered structurally weak. One of the most significant findings is that, on average, 57 per cent of Albania’s territory is uninhabited. The analytical document notes that the country no longer has the same population distribution it had in 2014, when the current administrative-territorial division was introduced with the aim of creating larger and more efficient municipalities. “Some areas have grown, while others have lost a significant share of their population,” the report says, arguing that some municipalities are struggling to secure sustainable finances, qualified staff and adequate administrative capacity. The Socialists have submitted a bill to parliament proposing a new administrative-territorial map that would merge several smaller municipalities with larger neighbouring ones – without explaining how the proposed map would address these underlying problems. The proposal has faced opposition from residents in the affected areas. Some fear mergers will leave them with even more limited access to public services.

headline: Kosovo’s LDK Drops Demand to Choose President in Bid to Resolve Crisis
author: Perparim Isufi
article_body: LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku addresses media on August 13, 2026. Photo: BIRN . The opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, said on Thursday it had withdrawn its demands to name the country’s new president in an attempt to end the political deadlock that has paralysed Kosovo since parliamentary elections in June. Lumir Abdixhiku, the LDK leader, said that while talks with the poll-winning Vetevendosje party’s leader Albin Kurti over a government partnership had not yet produced results, he was offering new talks about the election of a new president – which is crucial to avoid new parliamentary polls. “From this moment, no one has any reason, alibi or the right to delay the inauguration of parliament, the formation of the government and starting negotiations on a new president. We are late and should not waste any more time,” Abdixhiku said in a video message after a meeting with the party’s parliamentary group. “The constitutional uncertainty is a reality we cannot ignore … The crisis does not seem to have an end and it’s getting worse and worse,” he added. “We are ready to discuss the election of a president who defends our republic’s interests and its constitution, represents people’s unity and exercises the constitutional responsibilities. We are not asking for any posts or any political compensation in return,” he continued. In the June elections, Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, well ahead of the Kosovo Democratic Party, PDK, which won 22. The LDK won 18 seats and has until now insisted on having the president’s post, which Vetevendosje has deemed a “disproportionate” demand. Kurti will likely obtain a simple majority in the Assembly to form a new government, by again relying on the support of MPs from various ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk, Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs. However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved; the parties still need to agree on the election of a new president within two months of the inauguration of the new parliament, or it will trigger another election. Speaking on Friday, Kurti did not specifically say if he will accept the LDK offer, but welcomed Abdixhiku’s willingness to include other parties in negotiations over the presidency. “We are open to further discussions in order to come to a name or names [for the presidency], someone who is out of the current political scene, out of daily party polemics, and who is a unifying figure,” Kurti said. “We want to agree in advance in order to avoid new elections. The election of a parliament speaker and a cabinet is not a challenge, so we have to agree on the election of a president,” he added. Meanwhile a group PDK MPs protested on Friday for the second day in a row in front of acting premier Kurti’s office, demanding the resumption of parliament’s inaugural session. This was interrupted last Saturday when Kurti asked for “more time” to discuss the issue of a new president with other parties. So far, Abdixhiku and Kurti have met twice but have not found a common ground on new institutions. In his video address, Abdixhiku disclosed that the LDK was offered three ministries in Kurti’s next cabinet – “a disproportion we could not afford”.

headline: Montenegro Signs Deal With China to Extend Controversial Highway
author: Ivan Ivanovic
article_body: Montenegro has yet to rid its main telecoms networks of Chinese-manufactured equipment despite pressure from the United States and the European Union and pledges from the government to do so, BIRN can reveal. In November last year, the US State Department warned that the presence of untrusted vendors in Montenegro’s critical infrastructure posed a security risk to the country and its NATO allies. At the time, Economic Development Minister Nik Gjeloshaj said he would propose the mandatory removal of equipment made by Chinese Huawei and ZTE, identified by the European Commission in mid-2023 as posing “materially higher risks than other 5G suppliers”. According to BIRN’s findings, however, no such demand has been made. Montenegro has three mobile operators: Crnogorski Telekom, owned by Deutsche Telekom from Germany, One Crna Gora, owned by Hungarian 4iG Plc, and M:tel Montenegro, owned by Serbia’s state-owned telecoms company Telekom Srbija. All three use Chinese equipment, according to the Electronic Media and Postal Services Agency, EKIP, Montenegro’s independent communications regulator. The core network of One Crna Gora, for example, relies on equipment from ZTE, while its radio access network including the 5GNR network uses Huawei equipment. “To date, the Agency has not received any information from the competent authorities indicating that any equipment, device, or project poses a risk to Montenegro’s national security,” EKIP told BIRN. “For these reasons, it has so far not contested any request or project, nor banned the use of any communication equipment.” Vuk Vuksanovic, a foreign policy lecturer at King’s College London, said it was likely only a matter of time before Montenegro at least restricts the use of Chinese equipment in its 5G network. “It is highly probable that at some point, Montenegro will – perhaps not entirely replace or end partnerships with companies like Huawei – but deny them projects regarding the 5G spectrum,” he told BIRN. “However, we cannot predict that cooperation will vanish completely.” Gjeloshaj’s ministry did not respond to a request for comment. Security concerns A logo of Huawei Technologies Co on a phone screen in front of European Parliament in Brussels, March 2025. EPA/OLIVIER HOSLET For years, the US and EU have warned of security and privacy risks posed by Chinese telecoms equipment, arguing that the likes of Huawei and ZTE are vulnerable to pressure from the Chinese state to assist in cyber-espionage. The US Federal Communications Commission formally designated Huawei and ZTE as national security threats in 2020; US intelligence services have also warned of risks from Chinese cyber operations targeting telecom networks and supply chains. Montenegro’s 2024 Law on Electronic Communications liberalised the telecommunications market but allowed the government to restrict the procurement and use of equipment from manufacturers deemed harmful to national security. Draft amendments to the law, published in March , envisage the possibility of “different conditions” being applied to companies outside Montenegro and the EU, “when justified and necessary to protect public order, national or internal security, or public health”. The US embassy in Podgorica said Washington encourages Montenegro “to assess the security implications of its telecommunications infrastructure and consider trusted alternatives that protect sensitive data and critical networks”. For its part, the Chinese embassy said no one would benefit from such a move. “Chinese enterprises have not only provided quality products and services to people of all countries across the world, but also contributed to local and social developments as well as employment, and this is widely welcomed by various countries,” the embassy told BIRN. “Politicising trade issues will only disrupt normal technological exchange and cooperation and does not serve any party’s interest.” None of the three big mobile operators in Montenegro responded to requests for comment. Telecommunications expert Aleksandar Mastilovic said the wholesale replacement of such equipment is no small task. “Financially, replacing the core and radio access network is the heaviest burden,” he said. “For a small market like Montenegro’s, the problem is amplified because operators lack the economies of scale enjoyed by major European players, making the unit cost of migration relatively higher.” “Without some form of state or European support, a portion of that cost will inevitably trickle down to subscribers.” Mandatory removal Customers take photos of the ZTE Open mobile phone at a store in Madrid, July 2013. Photo: EPA/JAVIER LIZON Canada banned Huawei and ZTE from national telecom networks in May 2022, while Britain outlawed the purchase of new Huawei 5G equipment in 2020 and ordered its complete removal by the end of 2027. In 2024, Germany required operators to remove all critical Huawei and ZTE components from the 5G core by the end of 2026, and critical management systems in access and transport networks by the end of 2029. And in January, the European Commission proposed a revision of the Cyber Security Act to make the 5G Toolbox guidelines binding and set member states a three-year deadline to strip high-risk vendors from their ICT infrastructure. “Since not all EU member states approached the protection of critical infrastructure from untrusted vendors in the same way under the 2020 guidelines, a procedure is underway to adopt new measures that will be binding for all EU member states,” said Montenegro’s EKIP. “If adopted, they will require the removal of untrusted suppliers’ equipment from all network segments within 36 months.” Mastilovic warned that mandatory 5G replacement could slow down development, as operators redirect budgets from expanding their networks to replacing existing infrastructure. “But long-term, it doesn’t have to mean poorer quality, and European experience tells us a lot here,” he said. “Denmark switched to trusted vendors when upgrading to 5G and today has the best 5G coverage in the EU, proving that the transition does not have to come at the expense of performance.” “The real dilemma for Montenegro is neither ignoring the risk nor an abrupt, unplanned removal, but a clear, phased, and regulatory-driven plan that starts with the most sensitive parts of the network and addresses upfront who bears the cost.” US-China fight for dominance A woman passes by ZTE booth during Big Data Expo in Guiyang, China, May 2019. Photo: EPA/ALEKSANDAR PLAVEVSKI According to Vuksanovic, the US and China are in a fight for dominance of technological standards, saying that “whoever controls the standards controls the market”. “In this context, the 5G spectrum is seen as the newest and strategically most important form of wireless communication,” Vuksanovic told BIRN. “Numerous systems crucial to the economy and the functioning of society in the 21st century will depend on it, which is why the question of who will dominate this technology is increasingly being raised.” He believes the 5G issue is not just about economics, but security and data control: Western countries fear that Chinese tech giants, due to their close ties to the state, could grant Beijing access to sensitive information. Mastilovic said the core issue is not proven misuse, but the architecture of the technology itself. When a single vendor controls both the core and the access network, he said, the operator and the state gradually lose technical and negotiating autonomy. “A modern network, especially its core and management systems, is not a static box that you install once and forget,” Mastilovic told BIRN. “It constantly receives software updates and remote maintenance from the manufacturer. The moment that manufacturer is legally subject to a jurisdiction that can compel it to cooperate with its intelligence services, the ability to access traffic, manipulate it, or disrupt service exists at the architectural level, regardless of whether it has ever been exploited.” “That is precisely the point of the security logic warned about by NATO, the US, and the European Commission – it doesn’t start from intent, but from capability, because a state cannot base its critical infrastructure on the assumption of goodwill.”
