headline: US Right-Wing Heritage Foundation Promotes Changes to Bosnia’s Peace Agreement
author: Irvin Pekmez
article_body: Bosnia and Herzegovina was the only topic of the lobbying meeting between Paul McCarthy, from the influential US right-wing think-tank Heritage Foundation, and the right-wing Portuguese MEP Antonio Tanger Correa, held in Brussels in March. BIRN can reveal that the two men discussed the controversial idea that certain researchers at the Heritage Foundation have been promoting – a revision of the Dayton Peace Agreement, which ended the 1992-95 war. In response to BIRN, Correa’s office said that the MEP emphasised that a new approach to Bosnia and Herzegovina is needed and revising the framework established by the Dayton Peace Agreement should be a priority. “Thirty years after the Agreement, such thinking is necessary given the profound changes in the international environment and the internal political and institutional dynamics of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” Correa’s office said in a written statement. “The goal of any such discussion must be to ensure more efficient, more representative, and more sustainable institutions and to support the country’s European future,” it added, stating the MEP has long been interested in Bosnia and Herzegovina, particularly given his mandate as EU Special Envoy for the Western Balkans in 2007. McCarthy, the senior research fellow for European affairs at the Heritage Foundation’s Margaret Thatcher Centre for Freedom, did not respond to BIRN questions by the time of publication. Correa is vice-president of the right-wing parliamentary group Patriots for Europe in the European legislature and the Heritage Foundation is behind the Project 2025 policy package, considered to be the ideological foundation for the second Donald Trump US presidency. BIRN analysis of the Transparency International’s database that maps meetings held between EU officials and politicians, NGOs and lobbying firms from the EU and non-member states, shows Bosnia and Herzegovina was a topic of a number of other lobbying meetings between those who support a revision of the Dayton accords. Heritage Foundation researchers seek change in Bosnia Max Primorac, a senior research fellow at the Heritage Foundation’s Margaret Thatcher Centre for Freedom. Photo: US House Foreign Affairs Committee hearing. The suggested revision of the Dayton Agreement to give Croats more political power via a third, Croat-led entity – a highly controversial idea in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where many see it as riskily disruptive – was promoted at an event organised by the Heritage Foundation earlier this year. TradFest was held in Zagreb in April 2026, described on its official website as “a festival of tradition and conservative ideas, opposed to so-called ‘progressive’ and militantly secularist ideas and policies that seek to destroy the original traditional, conservative, and Christian foundations of culture in Croatia, Europe, and the Western world”. One of the sessions at TradFest was “Bosnia and Herzegovina: A Failed State and the Necessity of a Third Croatian Entity”, at which a map dividing Bosnia and Herzegovina into three “republics” – Serb, Croat and Bosniak/Muslim – was presented. In February 2026, the Heritage Foundation published an article by Max Primorac, another senior research fellow at the Heritage Foundation’s Margaret Thatcher Centre for Freedom, titled “An Islamist State on NATO’s Border?” It claimed that Bosniaks in Bosnia and Herzegovina have “rejected Croat and Serb calls for political equality”, and called on political leaders in Sarajevo to “stop oppressing” Christians in the country. A year earlier, the Heritage Foundation published a report by Primorac claiming that the Office of the High Representative, the international overseer responsible for ensuring the continued implementation of the Dayton peace deal, is the main cause of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s political dysfunction and has become an “imperial administrator” undermining domestic sovereignty. This position overlaps with the long-standing stance of the Serb-led Republika Srpska entity and of Russia, both which dispute the legitimacy of the High Representative and seek the reduction or abolition of the Office’s powers. A month before Correa’s meeting with McCarthy of the Heritage Foundation, the Portuguese politician met Primorac to discuss the current situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the data published by Transparency International shows. Primorac did not respond to multiple inquiries sent to his office. Who is Antonio Tanger Correa? The office of Portuguese MEP Antonio Tanger Correa said he believes a new approach to Bosnia and Herzegovina is needed and that revising the framework established by the Dayton Peace Agreement should be a priority. Photo: EPA/Hugo Delgado. Tanger Correa was the Portuguese ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1996 to 1998. He currently serves as vice-president of the Patriots for Europe group in the European Parliament, which brings together nationalist, conservative, and right-wing parties from several EU member states. Among them are the far-right National Rally from France, as well as Fidesz, the party of former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, which strongly supported Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik. Correa’s European Parliament biography states that he is a member of the board of the Patriots for Europe Foundation, a think-tank foundation affiliated with the Patriots for Europe political ‘family’. In July 2025, he criticised the European Union’s 2023 and 2024 reports on Bosnia and Herzegovina because it mentions that Russia and China as unacceptable sources of influence in Republika Srpska, but there is no mention of “growing Islamisation in parts of the [Bosniak and Croat-led] Federation [entity]”. Correa also proposed deleting text from the European Parliament’s 2025 report calling on Republika Srpska authorities to respect the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its ruling on the entity’s Law on Foreign Agents, which critics saw as a way for Dodik and his allies to target NGOs and independent media receiving foreign funds. Correa further proposed removing portions of text condemning the “secessionist intentions” of Republika Srpska’s leadership. He additionally suggested removing explicit references to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in the context of EU foreign policy and sanctions against Russia, as well as Brussels’ concerns about malign foreign disinformation influence on Bosnia and Herzegovina. Although the final version retained the condemnation of Russia and disinformation from Moscow, the word “secessionism” was removed. BIRN could not confirm whether or not Correa personally influenced that decision. According to SRNA news agency, in September 2025, Republika Srpska leader Dodik described Correa as a “friend” and a “voice of reason” in the European Parliament. According to Dodik, Correa rejects “colonial dictates” toward Republika Srpska – a reference to decisions by the High Representative that have curbed the Bosnian Serb leader’s official powers. Bosnian Serbs meet with French right-wingers Thierry Mariani, then an adviser to French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, attended the Day of Republika Srpska celebration in 2022 at the invitation of Milorad Dodik, despite the state-level Constitutional Court having ruled the event unconstitutional. Photo: EPA/Christophe Petit Tesson. Analysis of Transparency International’s lobbying data at EU headquarters reveals other meetings at which Bosnia and Herzegovina was a topic. These meetings involved politicians from Republika Srpska and members of the European Parliament close to right-wing, sovereigntist or pro-Russian-oriented forces in Brussels. The database reveals that in April 2026 a meeting was held between the president of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, Nenad Stevandic, and Aleksandar Nikolic, an MEP from the French right-wing National Rally party. Other delegates from the Assembly at the meeting were Republika Srpska MPs Maja Dragojevic-Stojic, Mladen Ilic and Aleksandar Trnic, along with Bojana Kondic Panic, head of the Republika Srpska Representative Office in France. BIRN contacted all the participants for details, but none of them responded to requests for an interview. The stance of National Rally members toward Bosnia and Herzegovina has been known for some time — in January 2022, Thierry Mariani, an adviser to then leader Marine Le Pen, attended the controversial annual celebration of the Day of Republika Srpska at the invitation of Dodik, even though the state-level Constitutional Court had outlawed the event for being ethnically exclusive. Zijad Becirovic of the International Institute for Middle East and Balkan Studies (IFIMES) in Ljubljana argued that support for ethno-nationalist politicians who question the fundamental principles on which the Dayton Peace Agreement rests – sovereignty and territorial integrity – represents a serious risk. “The policies of Milorad Dodik, part of the radical ethno-nationalist forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the [Bosnian Croat nationalist party] HDZ BiH [Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina] and [its leader] Dragan Covic, which have political support from related structures in Croatia, but also certain ties to Russian interests, have for years sought to present themselves as a struggle for ‘internal autonomy’,” explained Becirovic. “However, their actual political goals often exceed the boundaries of the constitutional order and lead toward the blockading of institutions, the destabilisation of the state, and, ultimately, secession,” he claimed. The EPP and the Heritage Foundation HDZ Bosnia and Herzegovina leader Dragan Covic, European Parliament member Zeljana Zovko and Croatian Foreign Minister Gordan Grlic Radman. Photo: Croatian Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs. A report published in February by Germany’s Der Spiegel , Sweden’s Aftonbladet and the environmental campaign group BLOOM detailed what BLOOM described as “harmful links between the European conservative right and Trumpist circles”, indicating that some European parliamentarians have come under American influence as Washington attempts to shift the political balance in Brussels rightwards. BLOOM researcher Alessandro Mazzotti told BIRN that the Heritage Foundation’s isn’t just seeking political connections on the far right of the European parliament, but also within European People’s Party, EPP, which brings together centre-right parties and is the largest political group in the EU. The report also highlights a meeting between Manfred Weber, president of the EPP, Jorgen Warborn, a member of the Swedish Parliament, and representatives of the Heritage Foundation. “The Heritage Foundation acts as a kind of intermediary in this shift of the EPP toward a more radically right-wing position,” said Mazzotti. An important figure connecting people within this lobbying environment, Mazzotti claimed, is Croatian MEP Zeljana Zovko of the centre-right Croatian Democratic Union party, which is part of the EPP. He claimed that Zovko has opened many doors for the Heritage Foundation. Zovko provided support for the Heritage Foundation’s TradFest in Zagreb. “Over the past three or four years she has been one of the leading representatives in the European Parliament for the European People’s Party. Essentially the first point of contact between the EPP and Heritage. She was really the person who started this cooperation, this dialogue,” said Mazzotti. Zovko has publicly met with Heritage representatives on multiple occasions, including Primorac. According to Mazzotti, Zovko is the first person to have created the link between the Heritage Foundation and the EPP – a link that today influences cooperation between Brussels and the Trump administration. Zovko told BIRN that critical sentiment towards her is partly caused by her role in the EU’s trade agreement with the US, as well as her role as the EPP’s chief negotiator in Brussels’ talks with Washington. “I am the EPP negotiator, that is why I am also in the area of defence and trade and that is why all the attacks are there. I am the contact person for Congress and all the [American] foundations. I am the key person in the EPP for relations with everyone in the US Congress and I talk to all the foundations,” she said. “As the vice-president of the EPP group in charge of EPP diplomacy, my duty includes maintaining contacts with all the relevant interlocutors. I open the doors and that is my nature – you have to communicate with everyone, not only with Heritage and America First, but also with the left foundations,” she added. In her view, a revision of the Dayton Agreement is not currently a realistic option. “I advocate for full implementation, respect for the Dayton Agreement and the spirit of the Dayton Agreement. It is not being respected; if it were, Croats would have their own member of the presidency and they would have a fair electoral law,” she said. Critics have alleged that the election victory of the current Croat member of the tripartite Bosnian presidency, Zeljko Komsic, relied on more Bosniak voters rather than Croats, and hence does not represent the will of the Croat people in the country. However, as Zovko pointed out: “For a revision [of Dayton], you need to have the other two peoples [Serbs and Bosniaks] on your side. The Serbs would not agree to that, and the Bosniaks in this set-up would not agree to a more profound revision either.”

headline: Falling Water Levels on Danube Threaten Serbia’s Electricity Supply
author: Marina Zec
article_body: A fire blazing in Serbia’s Deliblato Sands for seven days has finally been brought under control, Milos Milenkovic, Assistant Head of Serbia’s Fire and Rescue Units Directorate told the state broadcaster RTS on Tuesday. The Deliblato Sands, Deliblatska Pescara in Serbian, is the largest continental sandy terrain in Europe, covering around 350 square km in southeast Vojvodina, Serbia’s northern province – a nature reserve nicknamed Europe’s Sahara. The wildfire broke out amid an intense heatwave and prolonged drought affecting Serbia and much of the Balkans, with temperatures reaching around 40 degrees Celsius. The hot and dry conditions, coupled with strong winds, have significantly increased the risk of wildfires and complicated firefighting efforts. Two people attempting to fight the blaze at Deliblato Sands. Photo: Uros Arsic According to Milenkovic, the fire in the Deliblato Sands and another on Mt Stolovi, near the central town of Kraljevo, have not been spreading since Monday. “Most importantly, there are no residents or settlements at risk at either location, and protecting them remains our priority,” Milenkovic told RTS on Tuesday. Fires at Deliblato Sands. Photo: Uros Arsic Milenkovic added that the tough terrain is the main factor hampering firefighters’ work, as large parts of the Deliblato Sands are inaccessible to fire engines, trucks and even off-road vehicles. The cause of the fire still remains unknown and authorities have announced an investigation. Tackling the blaze in the forest at Dubovac. Photo: Uros Arsic Milenkovic explained that the sandy terrain also prevented firefighters from reaching the hotspots and directly tackling the flames. “The high concentration of smoke and combustion products, as well as the heat, are all factors making the operation more difficult. But no residents are at risk and there have been no fatalities,” he said. Locals providing aid in fighting fires at Deliblato Sands. Photo: Uros Arsic More than 1,500 hectares of forest and low vegetation have been burned in the special nature reserve, according to official data. The Deliblato Sands was not the only part of Serbia affected by fires. Major fires were also reported around Kraljevo, including on the Zaracke Mountains and Mt Stolovi, as well as in the Maglic-Usce area, while fires were reported around Zajecar and Knjazevac and on Stara Planina. “In the past two to three days alone, we have had more than 300 fires across Serbia,” said Luka Causic, the head of the Interior Ministry’s Emergency Situations Sector. Two men who participated in fighting the fires at Deliblato Sands. Photo: Uros Arsic Although the fire has been brought under control, firefighters, emergency services, forestry workers and volunteers remain on alert due to strong winds. Several settlements within the nature reserve, particularly Dubovac and Sumarak, were threatened by the fire but are now safe.

headline: Week in Review: Hopes, Schemes and Stand-Offs
author: Milos Damnjanovic
article_body: Good and bad vibrations President of Moldova Maia Sandu delivers her speech at a briefing in the presidential palace in Chisinau, Moldova, 29 May 2023. Photo: EPA-EFE/DUMITRU DORU Good news from Brussels came for Moldova on June 22, when an EU-Moldova summit saw the opening of the first cluster of negotiating chapters in Moldova’s EU accession negotiations. Spanning “fundamentals” – such as the rule of law, functioning of democratic institutions and judiciary – the cluster is the first step towards opening other accession negotiating chapters. Moldova is optimistic about making quick strides in its EU accession process. But while the government talks up the prospects of catching up with Montenegro, which hopes to join by 2028, most experts feel membership in the next decade is a more realistic scenario – should everything go according to Moldova’s plans and wishes. Meanwhile, the clouds are appearing, with a scandal over the employment of President Maia Sandu’s cousin in a lucrative public-sector job. Read more: ‘Milestone’ Opening for Moldova’s EU Talks – But Harder Work Lies Ahead (June 26, 2026) Read more: Relatives’ Job Scandals Cause Trouble for Moldova’s Anti-Graft President (June 30, 2026) Vucic’s plans Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic at a rally of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in Belgrade, 27 June 2026. Photo: EPA/ANDREJ CUKIC Amidst a busy European news agenda, it takes a special effort for Serbia to break into the continent’s headlines. Yet the announcement by President Aleksandar Vucic at a political rally that he plans to resign as president – “soon”, but it’s not clear when – certainly grabbed the attention of international media. In his opinion piece for Balkan Insight, Filip Svarm tries to decipher Vucic’s future plans. It stretches the imagination to think that he might become a private citizen. So, what are his options? Read more: What are the Secrets Behind Serbian President Vucic’s Resignation Pledge? (June 30, 2026) Squaring off US President Donald Trump with US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the White House, 21 June 2025. Photo: EPA/Carlos Barria/Pool. With much of the globe focused on the World Cup under way in North America, other bilateral contests are gaining less attention. One pitches the US against the EU, which are sparring across the Balkan region. In her Letter from Washington column, Jovana Djurovic looks at the ongoing standoffs. Most notably, in Bosnia, the US and EU are at loggerheads over the appointment of a new High Representative. A dispute over a luxury tourism development in Albania meanwhile is pitting not just these two actors against each other, but also members of the extended Trump family and Albanian society. Read more: Letter from Washington: US and EU Square Off Over Balkan Assets (June 29, 2026) Unprecedented turbulence Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama at a press conference, 2 June 2026. Photo: EPA/MALTON DIBRA Albania continues to be rocked by protests against a luxury tourism development project in which the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama is accused of bending laws to pave the way for the project, which is linked to Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law. This is not the only turbulence the country is experiencing. While previous protests against the Rama government have come and gone, few can remember when such opposition and criticism have come also from within the Socialist Party, since Rama took it over more than a decade ago. In the latest expression of unease among the Socialists, Marjana Koceku, the youngest MP in parliament, has left the party to become an independent – and joined the protests. Will Rama take notice? Read more: Albanian PM’s Response to Protests Causing Unease Within His Own Party (July 1, 2026) Deja vu Acting Prime Minister of Kosovo and leader of the Vetevendosje party Albin Kurti celebrates with supporters in Pristina after the elections on June 7, 2026. Photo: EPA/Georgi Licovski. With the final election results in Kosovo soon to be certified, the clock will begin counting down for a new government and president to be elected. However, it was precisely the failure to bridge the political divide and elect a new president that triggered the last parliamentary elections on June 7. Acting Prime Minister and Vetevendosje leader Albin Kurti described those early elections as unnecessary. But many observers fear an inability on all sides to strike a political compromise will lead to yet another election in the autumn. Read more: After ‘Unnecessary’ Polls, Kosovo Parties Ponder How to Avoid Another Crisis (June 26, 2026) Winless streak A bus stop with electoral posters depicting former Kosovo President Vjosa Osmani (L) and LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku in Pristina, 5 June 2026. Photo: EPA/GEORGI LICOVSKI Founded in 1989, the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, is the oldest political party representing ethnic Albanians in Kosovo. Its founder and former leader, Ibrahim Rugova, still holds a special “founding father” status among Kosovo’s Albanian majority. But has the party lost its winning touch? While it slightly improved its seat tally in the last elections, it remained stuck in third place. In the aftermath of the elections, a crisis has erupted within the party, with some in the LDK’s ranks calling for a new leader to restore its fortunes. Read more: Winless Since its Founding Father Died, Kosovo’s LDK Party in Fresh Turmoil (June 29, 2026)

headline: Kosovo Serb Businessman and Politician Radoicic Indicted for War Crimes
author: Perparim Isufi
article_body: This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp Milan Radoicic. Photo courtesy of N1. Kosovo’s Special Prosecution on Thursday said it has filed an indictment charging 20 people it suspects of committing war crimes against civilians in the western town of Gjakove/Djakovica during 1999. BIRN has learned that Milan Radoicic, a well-known Kosovo Serb businessman and politician, is among the suspects. The prosecution said that, according to the indictment, during the 1998-1999 war in Kosovo, the suspects, operating in different capacities of the Serbian Interior Ministry, “are accused of participating in the killing of 107 civilians during a large-scale military-police operation. “During this operation … the defendants initially separated the women and children from the men. The women were robbed, taking their gold jewellery, money and other valuables, while the men were executed, some in their homes and yards, some at a location known as ‘Taliqi Bridge’. The houses were also burned,” the Prosecution added. It proposed a trial in absentia for the defendants since they are all out of reach of Kosovo’s authorities. In April 2025, the Pristina Basic Court issued an arrest warrant for Radoicic and 19 others suspected of war crimes in May 1999 in Gjakova/Djakovica. The court said the Special Prosecution was investigating suspicions that from May 7 to May 10, 1999, the suspects were among uniformed Serbian military and police forces who “entered houses and using force and threats took everyone present out of their homes and separated the men from women and children. Later they killed 106 civilians of Albanian nationality. “After the war, their bodies were found in a mass grave in Batajnica in Serbia,” the court added. The court said it suspected that Radoicic and the 19 others “arrested and imprisoned 300 other civilians from the Albanian community and other ethnic communities, who were first kept in improvised prisons” and treated inhumanely. Many of these prisoners were transferred to prisons in Kosovo and eventually to Serbia, to be released after June 1999 with the assistance of the international community, the arrest warrant notes. “All the Albanian civilians and civilians and of other nationalities who lived in Gjakova were barred from their home via force and threats. First, all the houses of Albanians in Gjakova were robbed and then burned, causing material damage,” it added. The court noted that the suspects do not have addresses in Kosovo and are not accessible to the Kosovo authorities. Charged multiple times Radoicic is well known to the Kosovo authorities. They have charged him with multiple crimes, or listed him as the main suspect a number of times, but have not so far been able to bring him to court. Together with 42 individuals, he was charged with terrorism and endangering the constitutional order of Kosovo over the attack by armed Serbs on a police patrol in the Kosovo village of Banjska in September 2023, which left one police officer dead. Only three Kosovo Serbs have been arrested related to the attack. They have pleaded not guilty. Radoicic, who since fled to Serbia, took responsibility for leading the assault but insisted he did so without informing the authorities in Belgrade. At the time of the attack, Radoicic was deputy leader of Srpska Lista, the main Serb party in Kosovo, which operates closely in line with Serbia’s government, Serbia launched an investigation into Radoicic in September 2023, when the Belgrade Higher Prosecutor’s Office said it was probing him for organising an armed group, the unauthorised amassing of a large cache of weapons, which he transported to Kosovo, and for “serious crimes against general security”. Belgrade prosecutors questioned him in October 2023, when he reportedly claimed innocence. In April 2024 , the Kosovo authorities seized most of Radoicic’s property in the country. Prosecutors there also implicated him in a corruption scam in Brezovica in the Sharr Mountains National Park. He narrowly avoided arrest in 2022 when he tried to cross from Serbia into Kosovo, but turned back at the last second. Commenting at the time on the warrant issued against him, Radoicic suggested he was a victim of a campaign against Serbs in Kosovo. Radoicic was earlier named as the main leader of the criminal group that organised the murder of the Kosovo Serb politician Oliver Ivanovic, in 2018, together with businessman Zvonko Veselinovic. The men were never charged. In an interview with BIRN a few months before his murder , Ivanovic named Radoicic as the real power-holder in the Serb-majority north of Kosovo.

headline: Week in Review: Cocaine Busts, Changing Goals, Tourism Woes
author: Milos Damnjanovic
article_body: Wheel of fortune US President Donald Trump with the football World Cup trophy in the Oval Office, August 2025. Photo: EPA/ANNABELLE GORDON. Democracy promotion is out and energy and commercial interest are in. That, in a nutshell, sums up the Trump administration’s policy towards the Balkans. In her latest ‘Letter from Washington’ column, Jovana Djurovic takes a look at what the recently initiated “strategic dialogue” between Belgrade and Washington is all about. The latest twists and turns in Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik’s efforts to ingratiate himself with the MAGA world also receive scrutiny. Read more: Letter from Washington: US Seeks to Score Material Goals in the Balkans (July 28, 2026) What’s in a flag? Packages of cocaine decorated with Serbian flags, seized in Italy this week. Photo: Italian Financial Police. The Italian police’s seizure of a container of bananas from Ecuador, which concealed 650 packages holding 770kg of cocaine, on July 21 has created quite a stir. Even more intrigue and suspicion were sparked by the Serbian flag displayed on the packages. In his opinion piece for Balkan Insight, Sasa Djordjevic looks at what can be deduced from this. While a Serbian, or Balkan link, seems likely, he explains, the use of flags, or even pictures of celebrities, to mark drug packages is not unique – or proof of a link with Serbia. Read more: Serbian Flag on Cocaine Haul from Ecuador is a Clue – Not Proof (July 28, 2026) Faking it Albanians protest outside the Prime Minister Edi Rama’s office in May 2026. Photo: BIRN. Frustrated by the continuing protests which have gripped Albania – demanding, among other things, the resignation of his government – Prime Minister Edi Rama has taken to blaming social media for his troubles. Algorithms, Rama claims, are fuelling the “Flamingo Revolution” as the protests are nicknamed. BIRN’s own investigation suggests things aren’t so simple. Hundreds of fake social media accounts appear to have been created to attack the protest movement – and push the government’s own line. Read more: Fake Social Media Accounts Target Albania Protest Supporters (July 24, 2026) Much to be desired A statue of Justitia, also known as Lady Justice, in a Skopje court. Photo: Vasko Magleshov/BIRN. The European Commission’s latest rule-of-law report on North Macedonia does not paint a rosy picture of the state of its judiciary. A mix of political pressure and underfunding, it warns, is pushing the system to the brink of collapse. In our interview this week, we talk to Ivana Petkovska, a programme coordinator at North Macedonia’s leading judicial monitoring organisations. She points out that these are all familiar themes, which her and similar organszations have been warning about for years. The country’s legal framework, she says, is not as much of a problem as poor implementation of existing laws. Read more: North Macedonia’s Judiciary ‘Nearing Collapse’, Rights Monitor Warns (July 27, 2026) Soaring prices New apartment buildings under construction in Prague, April 2026. Photo: EPA/MARTIN DIVISEK. Across Eastern and South-eastern Europe, real estate prices have for some time been on an upward march. Good for owners but bad for buyers, many of whom are increasingly frustrated about their inability to buy homes. Many observers are puzzled about what really is behind this price boom. In his opinion piece for Balkan Insight, Velimir Sonje takes a look at the factors fuelling rising real estate prices in several countries of the region. Read more: What’s Driving the Real-Estate Price Surges in Eastern and South-East Europe? (July 27, 2026) Under threat The beach at Zvernec, site of a controversial planned resort project linked to Jared Kushner, where tyre tracks indicate the recent presence of heavy machinery. Photo: BIRN/Vladimir Karaj. Albania’s long, unspoiled coast has gone from relative anonymity to growing prominence, regionally and beyond. The latest saga over a luxury tourism development linked to Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, has further highlighted its place on the map. Alongside its undiscovered potential, however, our analysis shows that many problems dog Albania’s coastal areas. Among them, uncollected rubbish, untreated wastewater and construction debris threaten to undermine the country’s efforts to become the next big tourist destination on the Adriatic. Read more: On Albania’s Adriatic Coast, Tourism Ambitions Put at Risk by Pollution (July 28, 2026)

headline: Actress Sues Albanian Govt for Using Her Image for AI ‘Minister’
author: Blerina Gjoka
article_body: It was a cabinet choice that sparked headlines around the world: “Albania’s prime minister appoints an AI-generated ‘minister’ to tackle corruption,” reported the Associated Press in September 2025. The Washington Post ’s headline called it a “mischievous AI stunt”, while other news outlets noted that Rama’s announcement caused outrage among opposition MPs who accused him of trying to gloss over deep-rooted corruption problems. Named ‘Diella’, the AI minister is a virtual chatbot that had until last September been integrated into e-Albania, the government’s digital services platform. According to Rama, Diella was to serve as Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, with a specific task: to eliminate corruption from public procurement tenders – a key issue for Albania as it seeks to push forward its EU accession process. But a year later, the actual role of the bot ‘minister’ role remains unclear. At the Public Procurement Agency, where the bot’s skills were expected to be tested, work still appears to be at the preparatory stage. “There is a project to develop an AI-powered procurement system, but it is still in progress,” said Reida Kashta, the Agency’s director, when asked whether it had begun using AI in public procurement. According to Kashta, the agency has “just completed the drafting of the terms of reference”. This is a document that sets out the technical criteria for launching the tender that will select the company responsible for building the system. The public procurement system has for years been considered one of the sectors most exposed to corruption in Albania. Investigations by the Special Prosecution Office for organised crime and corruption, SPAK, have uncovered several cases involving schemes to manipulate tenders, in which winners had been predetermined before the procedures were launched. Contracts for the construction of roads, incinerators and other public investments have been subject to investigations over allegations of favouring economic operators and violating competition rules. The government’s ambition to integrate AI into the sector has been met with scepticism by both opposition politicians and public policy experts, mainly because of the security risks it entails, its lack of human capacity and various legal uncertainties. Opposition Democratic Party MP Klevis Balliu told BIRN that the use of AI could serve as an assisting tool for the administration, but could not replace the legal responsibility of institutions, nor guarantee the fight against corruption. According to Balliu, without a clear constitutional and legal basis, the creation of a virtual minister raises questions about who bears responsibility for decision-making, particularly in a sensitive sector such as public procurement. “Diella does not solve corruption. On the contrary, she raises a fundamental question: who bears responsibility for decisions influenced by a system that has no legally defined status?” Balliu said. He argued that a virtual system could help increase efficiency and identify irregularities, but “it cannot replace transparency, oversight and human accountability.” Public policy experts are also concerned about the use of AI in procurement without a comprehensive legal, institutional and technical framework in place. Alba Brojka, an independent digital policy expert, said artificial intelligence should not be treated as a “magic wand solution” to complex problems such as corruption, but only as a tool to increase efficiency and automate administrative processes. “Under [UN culture agency] UNESCO’s principles on the ethical use of AI, decision-making ultimately belongs to the expert or human, not the technology,” Brojka said. She sees this particular use of AI as “an excuse for a problem [corruption] that has existed for years”, and that what needs addressing first is the “legal gap and institutional capacity”. For Aranita Brahaj, head of the Albanian Institute of Science (AIS) the use of AI in procurement cannot be seen as a solution to tendering problems without first consolidating the legal framework and developing a new methodology to monitor the efficiency of such systems. “Albania still lacks a complete, secondary legal framework and, above all, this process is taking place at a time when public contracting is showing significant problems,” Brahaj said. Multiple challenges Reida Kashta, director of the the Public Procurement Agency. Photo: PPA. As part of its ambition to introduce digital systems into public policy, the government amended the Public Procurement Law in 2024 to include provisions allowing the use of AI in procurement processes. Advanced technology systems are intended to be used to help draft requirements at the pre-tender stage, support the dynamic purchasing system and digital auctions, operate the Digital Complaints System, and monitor contract implementation. Kashta, director of the Public Procurement Agency, said the law does now provide a legal basis for using AI in the procurement process. But experts believe these legal provisions do not provide a comprehensive framework capable of addressing all the challenges posed by the use of digital technologies. Meanwhile, a government strategy on the use of AI, and a new draft law on AI, which is still under consultation, have yet to be adopted. “These key horizontal [cross-sector] acts, beyond sector-specific legislation, should already be in force. Likewise, the institutions designated in the draft AI law should have clear powers and the capacity to implement them before we can effectively begin deploying AI in public procurement,” Brojka, the digital policy expert, said. According to her, this would ensure control mechanisms, independent monitoring, licensing and registration of AI systems. It would be done in line with categories established by law, algorithmic audits, as well as effective mechanisms for reporting violations of rights. But even the adoption of a new law would not resolve the security concerns surrounding the implementation of AI systems, because according to Brojka, the government’s ability to protect data remains inadequate. She said the Commissioner for the Right to Information and Protection of Personal Data has a “lack of capacity” to monitor private and public actors or various online platforms. “It would be an even greater challenge to ask the same institution to monitor data involving actors using AI, because that is not realistic,” she added. Brojka cited “multiple challenges” in applying AI systems to public policy and calls for the deployment of AI to go hand in hand with institutional accountability and transparency. These challenges include the lack of an analysis defining specific problems the technology is expected to solve, the quality of the data, and the Public Procurement Agency’s capacity to understand, train and monitor the models. She also stresses the need for clear methodologies for responsible use and auditing, emphasising that, regardless of AI assistance, responsibility for final decision-making in procurement must remain with humans. “All of these are challenges that the PPA still needs to address, and it appears that institutions do not yet fully understand this preparatory cycle. Instead, they seem to be driven by a political narrative that is far from the conditions that need to be met for the responsible use of AI.”. Brahaj, the head of the Institute of Science, also warns that implementation will take time and require monitoring. Equally important, she says, is how algorithms for evaluation, qualification and risk detection will be applied in tendering, and how prepared businesses are to compete and appeal decisions under conditions where AI is being used. Internal auditors and Albania’s Supreme Audit Institution, KLSH, as the external auditor, will also need to develop a new methodology. “Otherwise, this will remain a reform marked by failures, in which Albanian institutions will simply create a set of problems and defects that will serve as a laboratory for others to learn from,” Brahaj concluded. Diella sparks political and legal controversies Opposition MPs erupted in anger during a parliament session in September 2025 when Prime Minister Edi Rama presented a ‘speech’ by AI ‘minister’ Diella. “I’m not here to replace people, but to help them,” the AI entity – an avatar resembling a woman wearing traditional Albanian dress – ‘said’ in a video that was screened to the legislature. Opposition Democratic Party MP Gazment Bardhi raged that “the truth is that Edi Rama’s Diella is a propaganda fantasy. Corruption and organised crime are the reality.” In a separate controversy, the actor who voiced Diella in the bot’s previous existence as a digital assistant on the state’s e-Albania digital services portal, launched a legal case against state institutions because she said her image was used as the face of the public procurements ‘minister’ without proper permission. Actor Anila Bisha claimed that she only had a contract for her image to be used for the digital assistant, not for the new role. “I have nothing to do with Diella as minister and no one asked me about that,” she said. Bisha sought an immediate moratorium on the use of her voice and image, which a court rejected. On September 22, the court will start considering her case for a full ban on using her voice and image for Diella.

headline: ‘Consent is Key’: Bulgaria Accused of Coercion Over Syrians’ ‘Voluntary’ Deportations
author: Tommi Siviero
article_body: A young man is slumped against a wall in the corner of a room, next to a bunk bed. The floor in front of him is covered in blood, as are his face and legs. The disturbing scene features in footage viewed by BIRN, among several videos and images documenting the aftermath of what detainees describe as mass police violence at the Pastrogor detention centre in southeastern Bulgaria, near the Turkish border. Three men currently held there told BIRN that a special police unit beat detainees all over the facility, leaving some with broken hands and fingers and head wounds. At their request, BIRN has not published the images because the victims fear repercussions if their identities are revealed. Sources who spoke to BIRN allege the violence took place on July 26 after two people escaped from the detention center during a protest. The same event was also described in an August 7 press release issued by the activist collective, Collettivo Rotte Balcaniche. Some 28 kilometres from the Turkish border and located in the vicinity of other migrant hosting centres , Pastrogor had served as an open camp since 2012, processing asylum applications, until December last year, when it was transformed into a detention centre under the European Union’s new European Pact on Asylum and Migration. The pact entered into force on June 12. Since then, when there were just a few people in the camp, its population has soared to more than 220, activists say. Under the new pact, the vast majority of those arriving irregularly at the EU’s external borders will be detained for anywhere between seven days and 12 weeks while they undergo screening and asylum procedures. In some cases, such as those of people awaiting repatriation or transfer to a third country, their detention may drag on even longer. Expressing deep concern about the accounts of violence, Italian MEP Cecilia Strada told BIRN: “This isn’t the first time we’ve heard reports of violence against migrants by Bulgarian police forces.” What went on? A satellite image of the Pastrogor detention centre. Photo: © 2026 Airbus/Google Earth. Before the alleged violence, activists say protests had been going on for weeks against conditions at Pastrogor and the act of detention. According to Collettivo Rotte Balcaniche, “in reaction, at least one person was beaten up by a police officer, detained at the police station, and forced to sign a pledge not to take part in any future protests”. The situation came to a head on July 26, when Collettivo Rotte Balcaniche organised a demonstration outside the centre. Refugees and migrants joined in from inside. One of the videos seen by BIRN shows nine migrants in a small room screaming “open camp” and a number of activists standing on top of a car near the perimeter of the facility. The protest was peaceful, the activists say. Speaking on condition of anonymity, a Moroccan detainee told BIRN that two men – from Turkey and Tunisia – escaped. Other sources confirmed this. “Then a policeman came and spoke to me in English, telling me to tell my friends to go back to their rooms upstairs because the rapid response team was coming, and if they found us in the square, things would get worse,” the Moroccan man said. “Everyone understood the situation. It was dangerous, so we returned to our rooms quietly.” It is unclear which police unit the man meant by ‘rapid response team’. However, descriptions offered by migrants and refugees suggest the officers may have been part of the Bulgarian Gendarmerie. According to BIRN sources inside the detention centre, the officers were dressed in full anti-riot gear, with masks, batons and stun guns. They were accompanied by regular policemen. The sources say there were around 30 to 40 in total. “My friend and I were in the first room,” the Moroccan man said. “One of the masked men, holding a weapon, opened the door and said, ‘Get down! Get down!’ When I laid down on the floor, about 15 policemen entered the room and started beating us with batons. I thought it was the end. They beat me until I lost consciousness. They injured my friend’s head. They beat us mercilessly. I’ve never been beaten like that in my life. They went through all the rooms like that.” Two other detainees, from Morocco and Pakistan, confirmed the account. All sources BIRN spoke to stressed that beatings were meted out indiscriminately, across the facility. Collettivo Rotte Balcaniche said that surveillance cameras were turned off before the violence began, but offered no evidence. ‘Drenched in blood’ The second Moroccan man said officers also destroyed any phone they found, “so that we don’t publish photos of the beating”. But images and videos have emerged. Those seen by BIRN show at least eight different people with serious injuries, including two with bleeding head wounds. One man was drenched in blood. The Pakistani detainee said he knew of at least 18 injured. “They treated us brutally, as if we were criminals and not asylum seekers,” he said, speaking, like the others, on condition of anonymity. After the beatings, the first Moroccan man said he and 11 other people were taken outside. “They started hitting and cursing and pouring water on us,” he said. “I felt hysterical, I felt like I was suffocating.” He said the physical and verbal abuse continued at a nearby police station until the following day. “They said, ‘If you don’t like the food, don’t eat it. Don’t do this. Don’t speak.’ They forced us to sign pledges and told us, ‘If you don’t like this treatment, go back to your country.’” ‘European standards’ Turkish border soldiers monitor the repair of a protective fence at the Bulgarian-Turkish border near the village of Matochina, November 2021. Photo: EPA/VASSIL DONEV Bulgaria’s State Agency for Refugees told BIRN that the Interior Ministry, under which the agency operates, is responsible for security at the Pastrogor centre, but stated that “the material and living conditions at the Temporary Accommodation Centre (TAC) in the village of Pastrogor meet the established European standards”. Without addressing the allegations of police violence, the State Agency for Refugees said it “recognises the existing risk of escalating tensions between different communities, which may be primarily triggered by differences in the ethnic and/or religious backgrounds of the persons accommodated, and timely measures are being taken in this regard.” Pastrogor’s mayor Ilian Iliev and the local police did not respond to requests for comment. In comments to the local website e-svilengrad.com , Iliev confirmed reports of unrest, but suggested the protest might have been a stunt to help a detainee escape. The Pakistani detainee told BIRN: “We don’t know what our crime is or why we are being kept here.” “We understand that if a person wants to apply for asylum in a country, they have the right to seek asylum. But keeping people in a closed detention camp like this is extremely cruel and unfair.” In the run-up to implementation of the European Pact on Asylum and Migration, critics warned about access to the new facilities for human rights monitors. The warnings proved prescient, said Strada, the Italian MEP. “If serious violations can already take place in these centres within European territory without witnesses, imagine what can happen when you move them outside.”

headline: Ticket Out: A Serbian’s Journey from Mercenary in Ukraine to Gangland Hitman
author: Jelena Zoric
article_body:
For years, Aleksandar Dinic kept a bullet as a souvenir of the war in Ukraine. Police found it among his belongings in January, when they arrested the 35-year-old Serbian citizen on suspicion of murder. His alleged victim, a 43-year-old man, was shot dead on January 16 at the foot of Mount Avala, on the outskirts of the Serbian capital, Belgrade. The dead man is believed to have been part of a Balkan drug cartel and was on trial at the time in Belgrade, accused alongside others of smuggling 324 kilograms of cocaine from South America to Europe. Organised crime prosecutors in Belgrade suspect that Dinic was hired as a contract killer by the Montenegro-based Kavac criminal clan, according to case files seen by BIRN. Since 2015, dozens of people have been killed in a gang war between the Kavac and Skaljari clans, which trace their roots to two neighbourhoods of the Montenegrin coastal town of Kotor. Fighting erupted after 300 kilograms of cocaine vanished from an apartment in the Spanish city of Valencia. Skaljari member Goran Radoman was among the first to die, shot dead in his Belgrade garage. Since then, the feud has gone global, claiming victims in Montenegro, Serbia, Turkey, Austria, Greece, Spain and other countries. Dinic had no direct involvement in the gang war, but he did have experience fighting with pro-Russian forces in eastern Ukraine and was on the lookout for some extra cash. Ukraine battlefield as recommendation
According to statements made under questioning, Dinic was put in touch with the Kavac clan by his marijuana dealer, whom Dinic told he was looking for work outside his employment in a betting shop. The Kavac member he met offered Dinic 100,000 euros to kill a man. Dinic was a petty criminal previously convicted on drug and theft charges. He also had proven battlefield experience, having fought as a mercenary on the side of Russian-backed forces in Ukraine’s east. His name appears in a database compiled by the unofficial Ukrainian website Myrotvorets , where he is listed as a fighter in an illegal armed formation operating in the Luhansk region of Ukraine’s Donbas. According to the website, he was added to the database in August 2015. Dinic’s target was Zivko Bakic, who at the time was under house arrest and wearing an electronic tag on his ankle. For one hour each day, Bakic was allowed to take a walk outside. Dinic spent days studying his routine, walking through the woods in the Belgrade suburb of Sopot. One day, Dinic told police and prosecutors, his car got stuck in snow and Bakic, oblivious to his intentions, stopped to help. The next day, at the same spot, Dinic emptied seven rounds into him from a Heckler & Koch submachine gun. Then he drove away along icy roads with Lana, his Siberian Husky. No prosecution for fighting in Ukraine
Under Serbian law, participating as a volunteer or mercenary in a foreign war is a criminal offence, punishable by between six months and five years in prison, even more for those who participate as part of an organised group or recruit others to do so. Dinic was never prosecuted for his activities in Ukraine, which, according to social media posts, date to 2014. It is not known how long he spent in the country. He has a long record of run-ins with the Serbian justice system, on charges including theft, traffic offences and drug-related crimes. On several occasions, Dinic underwent psychiatric evaluation. One of the lawyers who represented him said he believed Dinic’s experience in Ukraine had a defining impact on his personality. “He described the war in Ukraine to me as a slaughterhouse and a deception,” said the lawyer, who asked not to be named. “I don’t think he ever recovered from that period of his life, and I believe he saw and experienced horrific things there. He became an even lonelier person, living an increasingly chaotic life. He frequently changed apartments and jobs. He worked at a betting shop, as a food delivery driver, and at gas stations.” “His moods changed constantly, and he used marijuana almost every day, sometimes other drugs as well, and often drank heavily.” Another veteran of the war, who does not know Dinic personally, said it was “very likely” he suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder, PTSD. “War is a horrific thing,” said the veteran, who spoke on condition of anonymity. “Shrapnel and body parts are flying around you, and every minute you wonder whether you will be the next to die. No one comes back from that unchanged.” According to data received from the offices of the Higher Public Prosecutor in Serbia, covering the period 2014 to April 2026, 60 cases were initiated under the criminal offence of participation in a war or armed conflict in a foreign country under Article 386a of the Criminal Code and organising participation under Article 386b. At least 23 of those cases have been initiated since 2022, the year Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Before that, Russia had fomented armed rebellion in eastern Ukraine starting in 2014, the same year Moscow annexed Crimea. Prosecutors reported at least three convictions since 2022 based on plea agreements. Killing for money
Dinic went to ground but was eventually arrested while walking his dog. That was the only reason he ever left the safe house rented for him by the Kavac clan. He says he was never paid the 100,000 euros he was promised. At first, Dinic refused to answer his interrogators’ questions. Then he broke down and cried. He spoke of his worry for his dog and what would happen to her with him in prison. The authorities found the dog another home. Dinic’s court-appointed lawyer asked him how he felt when he returned from Ukraine. “ Well, for the first four months after I came back, I was almost never sober,” Dinic replied. “I was drunk most of the time, trying to come to terms with myself. I suppose some of it is still there, although I don’t know. It’s hard. It’s hard to answer that question. I think it’s hardest to talk about yourself right now.” Dinic is currently in pre-trial detention.

headline: Bulgarian Man Killed After Being Lured to Meet Teenager, Police Say
author: Svetoslav Todorov
article_body: Plovdiv’s historic old town area. Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Klearchos Kapoutsis. Police in Bulgaria’s second biggest city, Plovdiv, said on Thursday that they have made eight arrests over the death of a man who was lured by teenagers to a meeting with “a 17-year-old girl, posing as a 15-year-old” and then severely beaten up. Police told a press conference that the teenagers had concocted a scheme to track, lure and then attack alleged paedophiles, and then livestream the beatings. Their victim, who was assaulted on Tuesday at a site near Youth Hill, a location near many of the tourist sights close to the centre of Plovdiv, has been named as Georgi Kuzev. After being assaulted, Kuzev was discovered by passers-by and taken to hospital. Nova TV said he had suffered a severe brain injury and various fractures. He died several hours later. The incident was initially reported by media as having potentially been a homophobic attack , after other such attacks in Plovdiv in 2020, sparking outrage from LGBTQ+ rights groups. But the announcement at Thursday’s police press conference caused a U-turn in speculation around the case. Atanas Kalchev, mayor of Krichim, a small town near Plovdiv, said the victim was originally from Krichim. “The case is extremely serious and is characterised by a high degree of public danger due to the cruelty of the crime committed,” Kalchev said in a statement on Wednesday before the police announced the circumstances of the attack. “Even if the initial theories [about a homophobic attack] don’t get confirmed, this doesn’t take away from the weight of the crime,” Kalchev added.

headline: Kosovo Opposition Snubs Acting President’s Meeting Amid Parliamentary Crisis
author: Perparim Isufi
article_body: Kosovo’s Acting President Albulena Haxhiu meets political leaders in Pristina on August 18, 2026. Photo: BIRN. Kosovo’s opposition on Tuesday disregarded an invitation from acting President Albulena Haxhiu to a meeting with the country’s political leaders aimed at defusing the ongoing parliamentary crisis. The crisis centres around the inability of political parties to agree on a candidate for president. Under the constitution, failure to choose a new head of state will trigger new parliamentary elections. However, attendees at Haxhiu’s meeting were mainly allies of her own party, Vetevendosje. Instead of attending the meeting, a group of opposition MPs from the Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) and the Alliance for the Future of Kosovo (AAK) went to the Kosovo Assembly, as they have been doing every day, to put pressure on the provisional parliamentary speaker, Avni Dehari, to call the inaugural session of the Assembly. The assembly’s rules require the provisional speaker to invite MPs to a session every 48 hours until they elect a speaker. But the last time Dehari actually presided over a session was August 8, which lasted only a few minutes. Dehari insists he will not call a session until parties agreed on a new president. “This situation should alarm all of us. No election victory gives anyone the right to put themselves above the constitution,” Besa Kabashi Ramaj, a PDK MP, told her opposition colleagues at a makeshift meeting in the Assembly. Opposition MPs have been holding these makeshift meetings every day in an attempt to press Vetevendosje to call the inaugural session. In elections in June, Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, putting them well ahead of the PDK, which won 22. The Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK) won 18 seats and has insisted on having the president’s post, which Vetevendosje has deemed a “disproportionate” demand. Kurti will likely obtain a simple majority in the assembly to form a new government by again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs. However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved. The parties still need to agree on the election of a new president within two months of the inauguration of the new assembly, otherwise a new election will be triggered. Last week, LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku announced that his party is withdrawing its demand to hold the president’s post in order to ease the negotiations for the formation of new institutions. However, no meeting with Vetevendosje leader Kurti has been held since. On Monday, Abdixhiku announced that he is not interested in attending Haxhiu’s meeting because opposition parties claim that Haxhiu’s role as acting president has ceased with the start of this Assembly’s session and that her role can be resumed only if she is re-elected as assembly speaker. “The only meeting I could hold is with [Albin] Kurti. In our view, Haxhiu is only an MP, therefore we can talk only with those who are entitled to talk,” Abdixhiku said. “[Kurti] told us that he will meet with LDK soon,” Haxhiu told media after Tuesday’s meeting. “After all these months, we don’t need to guess what the lack of agreement would bring… If we don’t agree today, new elections do not guarantee that we will agree tomorrow,” Haxhiu said, referring to the possibility of new snap elections if the parties fail to choose a new president. The parliamentary polls would be the fourth in less than two years.

headline: North Macedonia Indicts Ex-Deputy PM Grubi Over Lottery Machines Purchase
author: Sinisa Jakov Marusic
article_body: North Macedonia’s former First Deputy Prime Minister, Artan Grubi. Photo: vlada.mk. Prosecutors in Skopje on Thursday charged Artan Grubi and seven others with abusing their official positions to enable the purchase of video lottery terminals that could not legally be put into operation, costing the State Lottery more than 8.2 million euros. Grubi is accused of allegedly pushing for the move in 2023 and 2024 while serving as first deputy prime minister, despite knowing that the procedure was illegal and that the State Lottery could never use the gambling machines. “The defendants, acting jointly during 2023 and 2024, took actions that exceeded the limits of their respective powers and duties, with the intention of causing harm to the legal entity the State Lottery,” the prosecution said in the indictment. The gambling machines were subsequently purchased but, according to the prosecution, were never used. Grubi has denied any wrongdoing. The indictment came days before a house-arrest order for Grubi is due to expire. Prosecutors have asked the court to extend his house arrest, while also seeking 30 days in detention for another of the accused, the former State Lottery director Perparim Bajrami, who remains at large. Grubi fled North Macedonia in December 2024 as authorities moved to investigate suspected wrongdoing at the State Lottery. An international call for his arrest was issued, and he remained outside the country for more than a year. Grubi initially denied that he was on the run, saying he had travelled to Kosovo for private reasons and would return after completing his obligations there. He eventually returned to North Macedonia in February this year and was arrested at the Blace border crossing while entering from Kosovo. He was released from custody the same day after prosecutors asked for house arrest instead of custody, arguing that most of the evidence had already been secured and citing concerns over his personal safety in detention. A court approved the measure, prompting widespread criticism over the relatively lenient treatment of a former senior official who had already fled the country once. Grubi, a senior figure in the now opposition, ethnic Albanian Democratic Union for Integration, DUI party, served as first deputy prime minister and minister of political system and inter-community relations from 2020 to 2024. In December 2024, the US State Department sanctioned him for alleged involvement in corruption .

article_body: Deadlocked again Kosovo MPs convene for the inaugural session of parliament on August 8, 2026. Photo: BIRN. Kosovo’s governance drama is beginning to border on the absurd. Weeks after the June election results were certified, two months after the elections were held, MPs have yet to elect a parliamentary speaker and deputies and, in doing so, constitute the new parliament. The winning party, Vetevendosje, has the votes to elect a new speaker, and indeed a new government. Photo: EPA/GEORGI LICOVSKI. As Montenegro’s EU accession process steams ahead, the country is preparing to align itself with the EU’s visa regime by introducing visas for Russian, Chinese, Turkish and Saudi Arabian citizens, among others, from November. Russian and Turkish visitors in particular account for a significant share of overnight stays in the country, comprising just over 20 per cent of the total, combined. The confused state of the Croatian-Serbian river border will likely be no exception, even if it remains a low-intensity dispute for now. Yet a potential source of bilateral tensions and headaches for some can become an opportunity for others. headline: Secrecy Surrounds Croatia’s Arrest of Alleged Serbian State-Linked Hacker
author: Marina Zec
article_body: Photo illustration: EPA/SASCHA STEINBACH. The Croatian and Serbian authorities are remaining tight-lipped over the arrest last week of a Serbian businessman named as Georgije V., 33, on suspicion of hacking into the computer systems of various Croatian state institutions and public agencies. The Serbian man is reportedly suspected of hacking into the Croatian Interior Ministry, the Central Register of Pension-Insured Persons, the Croatian Health Insurance Fund, the Croatian Regulatory Agency for Network Activities, the Croatian Pension Insurance Institute, the Croatian Tax Administration and the Croatian Automobile Club. Tomo Medved, the Minister of Croatian Veterans, was asked about the case on Friday but declined to provide details. “I would like to commend the entire security and intelligence system for its responsible and vigilant monitoring and protection of the interests of the Republic of Croatia. Given the ongoing proceedings, I cannot comment further than that,” Medved told journalists. Croatian daily Jutarnji list has reported that the arrest took place on July 28, when Georgije V. was on holiday in Croatia. He had arrived with his wife, two children and mother at a tourist resort on the Adriatic coast a few days earlier. Following his arrest, police searched his electronic devices, vehicle and accommodation under court orders. They seized items and digital data allegedly linking him to criminal acts, including two mobile phones and a laptop containing a large amount of data. The court ordered one month of pre-trial detention, despite the man offering 20,000 euros in bail money and his family home in Novi Sad as collateral. Croatia’s Chief State Attorney, Ivan Turudic, initially sparked public interest on Monday when he made a comment about a case related to national security. It was then reported by Jutarnji list that Turudic was referring to the arrest of an alleged hacker linked to Serbia’s Security Intelligence Agency, BIA. It is not known whether the suspect’s alleged access to the computer systems of various institutions and agencies endangered Croatia’s national security in any way, or what he did with any data he may have obtained. Nera Gajdarov Beg, the suspect’s lawyer, told Jutarnji list that the court’s custody order is being contested. “An appeal has been filed against the decision to order pretrial detention because we believe that not all legal requirements for such a decision have been met. At this point, I cannot provide details of the defence because the proceedings are in the investigation phase, which is secret,” Gajdarov Beg said. The Serbian authorities have not commented on the arrest so far. However, Serbian media have reported that Georgije V. is the owner of an active Novi Sad-based company specialising in computer programming and cybersecurity.
