headline: Police Probe Homophobia Motive for Murder in Bulgarian City
author: Svetoslav Todorov
article_body: The centre of Plovdiv, Bulgaria’s second city. Photo: Svetoslav Todorov Media reports say police in Bulgaria’s second biggest city, Plovdiv, have made several arrests after man in his thirties died after apparently being lured via to a meeting via dating app then beaten up in what has been described as a “cruel” and possibly homophobic attack. The victim was reportedly lured via a dating app to a site near Youth Hill, a location near many of the tourist sights close to the centre of Plovdiv, on Tuesday. The man was then badly beaten and later discovered by passers-by and taken to hospital. Nova TV said he had suffered a severe brain injury and various fractures. He died several hours later. The age of the victim has been reported by some sources as 37 and by others as 31. Some reports claimed the perpetrators were teenagers, both males and females, who livestreamed the beating on TikTok. The name of the victims has not yet been confirmed by the authorities. However, Atanas Kalchev, mayor of Krichim, a small town near Plovdiv, said the victim was originally from Krichim. “The case is extremely serious and is characterised by a high degree of public danger due to the cruelty of the crime committed,” Kalchev said in a statement on Wednesday. “Even if the initial theories [about a homophobic attack] don’t get confirmed, this doesn’t take away from the weight of the crime,” he added. Bulgarian LGBTQ+ rights NGO GLAS (Gays & Lesbians Accepted in Society) called for a “prompt, thorough and impartial investigation”. “Investigators are examining whether the crime was motivated by hatred related to the victim’s sexual orientation,” GLAS said. It noted that in 2023, sexual orientation was included in the Bulgarian Criminal Code as a factor in hate crimes. “If the investigation finds that the motive was indeed hatred based on the victim’s actual or perceived sexual orientation, the law should be applied to its full extent,” GLAS urged. In 2020, there were a series of homophobic attacks in Plovdiv , also connected to young members of anti-LGBTQ+ groups. This week’s case echoes the murder of 26-year-old Mihail Stoyanov back in 2008, who was killed in a park in Sofia. It became one of the most high-profile homophobic crimes in the country’s history and in 2022, the European Court of Human Rights censured Bulgaria over the case.

headline: As One Door Closes, Another Opens: Chinese Migrants Crossing the Balkans
author: Nino Bilajac
article_body: In recent months European officials have intensified talks with the authorities in the EU candidate state Bosnia and Herzegovina on the issue of harmonising its visa policy with Schengen Area regulations. Of particular concern to the EU is Bosnia's visa-free regime for citizens of Turkey, Russia, China and Saudi Arabia. Although it is formally treated as a technical requirement in the field of migration and border management, visa harmonisation is one of the most politically sensitive conditions affecting Bosnia and Herzegovina's European path. The government in Sarajevo is a close ally of Turkey, w hile the government in Republika Srpska is close t o both Russia and China. Visa-free tourists also bring much-needed income to the country. The existence of the request to eliminate visa-free status for the four countries has been confirmed by Bosnian and Herzegovinian Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic. Konakovic said that the EU is asking Bosnia and Herzegovina to introduce visas for citizens of certain countries, but that the authorities “cannot obey” all the demands of Brussels. “They criticised us for that. We explained that we cannot introduce visas for Turkey, and political partners from Republika Srpska would certainly not support the introduction of visas for Russia or China,” Konakovic said. In January this year, he announced that by the end of the year Bosnia would introduce visas for one of the countries with which it currently has a visa-free regime, but he did not specify which country. The European Commission has been warning the Western Balkan countries for years that an unharmonised visa policy could pose a security and migration risk. Commissioner for Home Affairs Ylva Johansson stated back in 2022 that candidate countries must harmonise their visa regimes with the European Union if they wish to maintain credibility in the accession process, warning that the EU would closely monitor deviations that could lead to increased migration pressures. Similar messages have been repeated in the European Commission’s annual reports on progress towards membership, as well as in reports on the visa suspension mechanism, which requires Bosnia to gradually align with the European list of countries whose citizens require a visa to enter the Schengen area. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs told BIRN that through the Stabilisation and Association Agreement it signed with Brussels, Bosnia and Herzegovina undertook the obligation to gradually harmonise its visa policy with the EU. “The European Union regulation establishes a list of third countries whose citizens must have a visa when crossing the external borders of member states. On this list are countries whose citizens can enter Bosnia and Herzegovina without the obligation to obtain visas, namely: Qatar, Kuwait, Azerbaijan, Turkey, China, Russia and Vanuatu,“ the ministry stated. It added that Bosnia and Herzegovina is obliged, over the coming years, to gradually introduce a visa regime for certain countries from this list, but that such decisions will require political consensus, which currently does not exist. Since 2025, the European Union has further tightened the rules of the Visa Suspension Mechanism, enabling responses in cases of increased undocumented migration, asylum abuse, security threats or significant deviations by candidate countries from the EU’s common visa policy. Because of this, Western Balkan countries, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, are under increased monitoring. The latest report by the European Commission on the visa suspension mechanism stated that Bosnia had regressed in its alignment with the EU visa policy in 2025. The commission noted that the country maintains seven permanent visa-free regimes with countries whose citizens require visas to enter the EU, while the number of seasonal exemptions increased from one to three. This raised the number of deviations between Bosnia’s visa policy and that of the EU from eight to 10. Economic reasons for deviation A group of Chinese tourists visiting Bosnia’s capital Sarajevo. Photo: BIRN. Although Brussels primarily views the issue through the lens of migration and security, in Bosnia it also has a significant economic dimension. According to data from the Agency for Statistics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, foreign tourists made 2.87 million overnight stays during the last year. Guests from Turkey accounted for 9.7 per cent of all foreign overnight stays, citizens of Saudi Arabia for 5.6 per cent, China for 3.8 per cent and Russia for about 0.8 per cent. This means that these four countries together make up roughly one fifth of all foreign tourist overnight stays in Bosnia. The dean of the faculty of political sciences at the University of Sarajevo, Sead Turcalo, believes that harmonising visa policy is an expected part of the process of joining the European Union, but warns that a complete and rapid introduction of visas could have significant consequences for the country’s economy. “The reason is simple. Bosnia and Herzegovina is not close to concluding negotiations and membership. Even from the moment the negotiation process is opened at full capacity, we have a multi-year process of harmonisation, opening and closing chapters ahead of us,” Turcalo told BIRN. “Therefore, it is not rational for Bosnia and Herzegovina to already take on the economic cost of full visa harmonisation, while at the same time not yet having the benefits of membership,” he added. He believes that Bosnia’s European integration process should not mean giving up its own economic interests without clear deadlines and compensatory mechanisms. “At this moment, a complete and rapid introduction of visas for these countries, especially for Turkey, Saudi Arabia and China, is not in the interests of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” Turcalo argued. The president of the Bosnian-Chinese Friendship Association, Faruk Boric, offered a similar view, arguing that abolishing the visa-free regime with China would do more harm than good. “We simply need a visa-free regime with China. Since the moment these benefits were introduced, the number of tourists has increased significantly,” said Boric. “I think we can only lose, we can gain nothing. We will not gain anything by introducing visas for China or Turkey,” he added. The European Commission did not respond to BIRN’s questions by the time of publication of this article.

headline: Kosovo Detains Man Suspected of Spying for Serbian Intelligence
author: Ardita Zeqiri
article_body: Fehim Sali, second left, at a court hearing in Pristina on August 14, 2026. Photo: BIRN Pristina Basic Court on Friday ordered 30 days of detention for a dual Kosovo and Serbia citizen, Fehim Sali, who is suspected of spying for Serbia’s intelligence agency, the BIA. It is alleged that he passed the BIA information about Kosovo officials, politicians and Islamist radicals, including potential recruitment targets, and received money in return. Sali, a resident of Kosovo’s southern Dragash/Dragas municipality, was arrested on Thursday at the Merdare border crossing point while entering from Serbia. He appeared before the Basic Court in Pristina on Friday. “The court’s assessment took into account the circumstances relating to the risk of absconding, the risk of influencing witnesses and evidence, and the risk of repetition or continuation of the criminal offence,” the court said in a statement. According to the prosecution file, Sali is suspected of “maintaining contact with BIA officers using four different mobile phones”, which were found during raids at his house on Thursday, alongside around 40,000 euros in cash. The prosecution file alleges that Sali “worked as a recruited agent for Serbia’s Security Information Agency, BIA, in exchange for material benefits”. The file alleges that he acted on the instructions of a senior BIA officer identified as Zelimir Matovic, nicknamed Zeljko. It alleges that Sali provided the BIA with information about Kosovo’s political situation and helped it identify officials of Kosovo’s own intelligence agency, the AKI. According to the case file, he photographed some of its officials to facilitate their identification. Sali is also accused of providing information about members of the radical Islamist Wahhabi movement as well as other people whom he allegedly proposed to the BIA officer as potential targets for contact and recruitment. According to prosecutors, Sali also “mediated matters and documents connected to Serbian state institutions and maintained contacts with people with political and social influence in Serbia and Kosovo, particularly members of non-majority communities”. The prosecution stated that he provided some of these people with “guidance on political activity, with the aim of gathering and transmitting information of interest to the BIA”. Prosecutors argue that these activities were carried out against the state interests of Kosovo and endangered its constitutional order and national security. The prosecution also alleges that the 40,000 euros found and seized during a search of Sali’s home came from his alleged activities on behalf of the BIA. According to the case file, the evidence against Sali includes his own statement. Prosecutors claim he described in detail his alleged activities, including how and where he communicated with BIA officials, exchanged information and provided assistance to the Serbian intelligence service. Prosecutor Bekim Kodraliu told media that Sali admitted having been recruited and maintained regular contact with BIA officials. “The suspect himself stated that he had been recruited and had ongoing contacts with BIA officials,” Kodraliu said. The case comes two months after another Kosovo espionage conviction involving Serbia’s intelligence service. In June, the Pristina Basic Court sentenced a Kosovo Albanian man, Hysri Selimi, a former Islamic State member, to six years in prison for espionage. Prosecutors said Selimi had provided the BIA with information about religious radicalisation in Kosovo, former members of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, and people who had joined Islamic State.

headline: US Right-Wing Heritage Foundation Promotes Changes to Bosnia’s Peace Agreement
author: Emina Dizdarevic Tahmiscija
article_body: Ahead of parliamentary elections in October, and with the Trump administration showing strong interest in energy projects in the country, the main Bosnian Croat party, the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina (HDZ BiH), has signed an agreement with the US government relations and strategic communications firm Mercury Public Affairs. The contract, which was publicly disclosed through the US Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) and signed on July 24 by HDZ BiH leader Dragan Covic, states that the engagement costs $30,000 per month, excluding taxes. Foreign policy journalist Harun Karcic, founder of the Initiative for Strategic Analysis, said the contract is connected to upcoming elections in which HDZ BiH is aiming for political dominance among Bosnian Croats - as well as “strong pressure from the US administration regarding the Southern [Gas] Interconnection – a project that Washington views as a key issue of energy security and reducing dependence on Russian gas in this part of Europe.” Karcic believes that through its engagement of Mercury Public Affairs, the HDZ BiH is seeking to promote its position that a new company should be set up in Mostar - the centre of Bosnian Croat political power, where the party has its headquarters - to manage the planned gas pipeline. The party is seeking to frame its wish as a matter of constitutional balance rather than an obstruction of a US strategic project, Karcic says. Political analyst Kurt Bassuener of the Democratization Policy Council think tank, views the contract as the HDZ BiH's formal entry into the lobbying game in the US and as an attempt to influence American policies toward Bosnia and Herzegovina in line with its agenda. He noted that Republika Srpska, Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Serb-majority entity, has made use of Washington DC lobbyists since 2007. The results of s uch lobbying was made clear last year when sanctions against Bosnian Serb political figures such as former Republika Srpska President Milorad Dodik, his family and others were lifted. According to Bassuener’s calculations, Republika Srpska has 15 entries in the FARA registry, which he considers excessive given that it is a territory of likely fewer than one million inhabitants. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in contrast, has only recently entered this lobbying sphere – without any significant results. “It is quite clear that the HDZ BiH wants to gain greater influence in the already favourable environment of the reactionary Trump administration ,” Bassuener told BIRN . In February 2026, the Heritage Foundation, a prominent Washington DC-based conservative think tank, publish ed an article by researcher Max Primorac titled “An Islamist State on NATO’s Border?” The article claims that Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina reject the idea of political equality with Serbs and Croats, and that the administration in Sarajevo should “stop repressing its Christian neighbours” – meaning the Serbs in Republika Srpska and the Bosnian Croats. The Heritage Foundation also published a report by Primorac in 2025 that claimed that the Office of the High Representative (OHR), the international overseer of the implementation of the peace deal that ended the 1992-95 war, is the ma in cause of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s political dysfunction and has become an “imperial administrator” that undermines domestic sovereignty. Bassuener said that within the European Union, much of this agenda can be pursued through the European People’s Party (EPP), of which Croatia’s HDZ is a member, together with its branch in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This plays a significant role in their agenda, he said, given that Bosnia and Herzegovina is effectively Croatia’s only major foreign policy issue. ‘American power for sale’ President of HDZ BiH Dragan Covic, member of the European Parliament Zeljana Zovko, and Croatian Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Gordan Grlic Radman. Photo: mvep.gov.hr. For political analyst Tanja Topic from Banja Luka, it is obvious that Covic listened to his political al ly Dodik an d followed in his lobbying footsteps. According to her, Dodik’s experience is valuable, and every opportunity to capitalise on American support for Christian values is being used. “Of course, the work of lobbying firms should not be equated with the positions of the State Department, nor should we blindly believe domestic spin masters who equate these activities with ‘friendship with Trump’,” Topic said. “The purpose of these activities is to lobby for the ‘Croatian issue in Bosnia and Herzegovina’, which implicitly points to a connection with the elections, while the second part concerns the biggest current US interest in BiH – the Southern Interconnection.” Adnan Huskic, a professor of political science and international relations at the Sarajevo School of Science and Technology (SSST), previously told BIRN that this mov e by HDZ BiH is l ogical. “It is clear that everyone has seen that American power is for sale,” Huskic said. “So they are doing this to increase their standing and their chances for any future plans.” Karcic says that what Covic wants from Mercury Public Affairs – crisis communications and public affairs experts who can navigate the corridors of Capitol Hill – is to promote the following argument: “We are not against American gas, we are for American gas, but we want it to be managed by an organisation based in Mostar in order to ensure institutional equality.” According to the signed contract, Mercury Public Affairs is also committed to strengthening the HDZ BiH’s relations with institutions and representatives of the United States, NATO, the European Union and “other relevant international stakeholders”. For Karcic, in the language of lobbying in Washington, this is a classic “pro-Western shield”. Karcic noted that the inclusion of a commitment to NATO, the US and the EU creates the impression for American decision-makers that the HDZ BiH is a stable Euro-Atlantic partner. He said this is crucial for the party because it neutralises accusations that its tactical partn ership with Dodik’s Serb nationalist party SNSD is weake ning the country’s pro-Western course. “This is an attempt to brand the HDZ in Washington as a bulwark of Western values in Bosnia and Herzegovina, conveying the message that internal stability – as they see it, through Dayton and the constituent peoples [Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs] – is actually a prerequisite for the overall security architecture of this region,” Karcic said. Bassuener considers the contract fairly standard and noted that it contains reference to the “equality of constituent peoples” and the “preservation of peace, stability, territorial integrity and the multi-ethnic character [of Bosnia and Herzegovina] “, as well as a target of presenting the HDZ BiH’s positions to the US government, elected representatives, the media and the wider public. “However, it is considerably less explicit than statements already publicly available regarding a third entity, the ‘discrimination’ against Croats, electoral reform and similar issues,” Bassuener said. Lobbying against Dayton Max Primorac, a senior research fellow at the Heritage Foundation’s Margaret Thatcher Centre for Freedom. Photo: US House Foreign Affairs Committee hearing. Representatives of the Heritage Foundation have lobbied members of the European Parliament, and one of these MEPs subsequently advocated for a revision of the Dayton Peace Agreement. The foundation also organised TradFest in Zagreb in April 2026, which was described on its official website as a “festival of tradition and conservative ideas, in opposition to so-called ‘progressive’ and militant-secularist ideas and policies that seek to destroy the original traditional, conservative and Christian foundations of culture in Croatia, Europe and the Western world.” One of the events at TradFest was titled “Bosnia and Herzegovina: A Failed State and the Necessity of a Third Croatian Entity”, where a map depicting the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina into three republics – Serb, Croat and Bosniak-Muslim – was presented. TradFest was supported by European Parliament member Zeljana Zovko, who is responsible for communications with organisations like the Heritage Foundation on behalf of the EPP. She told BIRN that she does not consider a revision of Dayton to be a realistic option at present. “I advocate for the full implementation and respect of the Dayton Agreement and the spirit of the Dayton Agreement. It is not being respected. If it were, Croats would have their own member of the presidency and would have a fair electoral law. To revise it, you need the other two peoples on your side. The Serbs would not agree to that, and the Bosniaks in this set-up would not agree to a more profound revision either ,” Zovko said. Croatian Foreign Minister Gordan Grlic Radman said during a visit to Bosnia and Herzegovina that Zagreb would “not get tired” of its demands to amend Dayton and would continue discussing with the EU and US the need for limited constitutional changes and amendments to the election law so that Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina could exercise their rights. Karcic says that with this move, the HDZ BiH is making it clear that it does not believe Bosnia and Herzegovina’s embassy in Washington DC or the Ministry of Foreign Affairs can or want to represent its specific political objectives. He said it shows the adoption of a model that has been used in Republika Srpska for years – where entity or party funds are used to hire FARA-registered agents to pursue a parallel foreign policy. “This is a shift toward a more aggressive, Western model of lobbying, where influence is simply bought on the market,” Karcic argued. “In the long term, when political parties conduct separate, private lobbying campaigns in Washington with competing narratives, this further undermines the cohesion of the state and creates an image among foreigners of a deeply fragmented society in which there is no minimum consensus on any strategic issue,” he concluded.

headline: NATO Peacekeepers’ ‘Transition’ at Flashpoint Bridge Alarms Kosovo Serb Party
author: Ardita Zeqiri
article_body: A Kosovo Police patrol car on the Iber bridge in Mitrovica, August 10, 2026. Photo: BIRN/Florinda Kelmendi. The NATO-led peacekeeping mission in Kosovo, KFOR, said on Monday that it had begun a gradual transition away from its permanent presence on the main bridge in the ethnically divided town of Mitrovica, citing “an improved security situation in Kosovo”. The town has been split into a northern, Serb-run half and a southern, Kosovo Albanian-run half, since the end of the Kosovo war in 1999, sparking numerous incidents since then. “In line with the improved security situation in Kosovo, this is part of the process for optimising KFOR’s posture,” KFOR told BIRN on Monday. “This process will be gradual, conditions based, and is being closely coordinated with all relevant stakeholders, including representatives of the Institutions in Kosovo and of international organisations, as well as with representatives of the Kosovo Police and the EU Rule-of-Law Mission in Kosovo (EULEX),” it added. However, after a Kosovo Police vehicle appeared on Monday on the bridge, Srpska Lista, the Belgrade-backed Kosovo Serb party, said it strongly opposed the withdrawal of KFOR members from the bridge and called for an urgent meeting with KFOR commander Ozkan Ulutas. “Given the extremely complex political and security situation, as well as the fact that the area around the main bridge has for decades been a site of serious tensions and conflicts, we believe that any decision that could affect security at this sensitive location must be made with the utmost care and with full consideration for the concerns of citizens,” Srpska Lista said. According to Srpska Lista, Kosovo Police “have failed to build the trust of the Serbian people through their actions. “Their conduct in numerous situations, including their support for actions that we consider unlawful and directed against the Serbian people and their institutions, has further deepened mistrust and the sense of insecurity among Serbs,” the statement said. Apart from the main bridge over the Iber/Ibar in Mitrovica, Kosovo’s government has opened two additional bridges connecting the southern and northern, Serb-run, parts of the city. Earlier on Monday, meanwhile, KFOR announced that it has begun a “gradual integration of Kosovo Police personnel into KFOR’s security architecture” at the Decani Monastery in western Kosovo, an important site for Serbian Orthodox believers. The mission said the move was part of a “broader process to optimise its security posture and will be implemented gradually and based on conditions on the ground”. KFOR noted that it “remains the first responder responsible for the Monastery site’s protection and will maintain a visible presence in south and north Mitrovica and in northern Kosovo”. The monastery, a UNESCO World Heritage site, has been under KFOR protection since the end of the war in Kosovo in 1999. The mission said it would maintain close cooperation with the Serbian Orthodox Church, Kosovo institutions, international organisations and the Serbian Armed Forces, in order “to safeguard mutual transparency, cooperation and trust, and to avoid misunderstandings”. “KFOR’s commitment to the security of the Visoki Decani Monastery and to the safety of all local communities is steadfast,” the mission said.

headline: Falling Water Levels on Danube Threaten Serbia’s Electricity Supply
author: Marian Chiriac
article_body: The Romanian government on Thursday urged households and businesses to reduce electricity consumption between 7 p.m. and 11 p.m. until the end of the month, to ease pressure on the power system during the ongoing heatwave. “Keeping electricity consumption as low as possible during the evening hours will not affect essential services, such as healthcare,” Romania’s interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan said. “We are going through a difficult period that could last another one to two weeks, and we are compelled to take these measures,” he added. The capital, Bucharest, has already reduced street lighting by one-third in the evenings and switched off illumination at landmark buildings and museums overnight to save electricity. Other cities have introduced similar measures. Earlier this week, the country’s largest energy-intensive companies, including car manufacturers, steel producers, fertilizer plants and other major industrial consumers, suspended operations or scaled back production to reduce pressure on the power grid. A prolonged heatwave and record-low water levels on the Danube have forced Romania to restrict water use for agricultural irrigation, disrupting river transport, tourism and the energy sector. The authorities have also shut down one reactor at the country’s only nuclear power plant, at Cernavoda, which relies on Danube water for cooling. Low water levels on the Danube are expected to continue affecting operations at the Cernavoda nuclear plant at least until mid-August. The government declared a nationwide energy alert on July 31, which will remain in force throughout August.
